The Convention defines “violence and harassment” as a range of unacceptable behaviours and practices that aim at, result in, or are likely to result in physical, psychological, sexual, or economic harm, including gender‑based violence. It obliges ratifying States to adopt comprehensive national laws, ensure effective enforcement, provide accessible complaint mechanisms, protect whistle‑blowers, and integrate prevention into occupational safety and health (OSH) systems.

Implementation is monitored through the ILO’s supervisory system: the Committee of Experts on the Application of Conventions and Recommendations (CEACR) examines periodic reports, and the Conference Committee on the Application of Standards (CAS) discusses cases of non‑compliance. The 2023 CEACR report noted that 22 of the 34 ratifying States had submitted their first detailed reports; common gaps included the absence of a clear legal definition covering all forms of harassment, limited coverage of informal‑economy workers, and insufficient data collection on incidence rates. The ILO’s “C190 Implementation Guide” (2022) provides a step‑by‑step roadmap: (i) legislative review and amendment; (ii) establishment of a national tripartite committee; (iii) development of sector‑specific codes of conduct; (iv) training for labour inspectors and judges; (v) creation of a confidential reporting hotline; and (vi) periodic impact evaluation.

Ratifying States have adopted diverse approaches. Canada amended the Canada Labour Code (2022) to include a standalone harassment provision and mandated employer‑led risk assessments. Germany extended its General Equal Treatment Act (AGG) to cover workplace harassment and introduced a statutory right to “psychological risk assessment”. South Africa promulgated the “Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Violence and Harassment in the Workplace” (2023), linking it to the Employment Equity Act. The ILO’s technical assistance programme, funded through the Regular Budget and voluntary contributions, has delivered capacity‑building workshops in 18 countries since 2021, focusing on labour inspector training and social dialogue mechanisms.

  • Assuming IDA graduation is automatic once the GNI threshold is crossed; the Board must still approve the transition and can extend it for fragility.
  • Treating the NDB’s equal voting shares as a guarantee of equal project distribution; project approval still requires a qualified majority and alignment with the Bank’s sectoral priorities.
  • Believing the MPIA replaces the Appellate Body permanently; it is an interim arrangement that expires once a reformed AB is operational.
  • Confusing GCF’s Direct Access with Enhanced Direct Access; the latter provides readiness grants but does not itself disburse project finance.
  • Overlooking that C190 requires ratifying States to cover informal‑economy workers; many national laws still limit protection to formal employment contracts.
  • Thinking the GCF replenishment burden‑sharing formula is based solely on GDP; it also incorporates historical emissions and capacity‑to‑pay indicators.
  • Assuming the NDB’s admission of new members automatically increases each founding member’s voting share; voting shares are re‑balanced only after a capital increase approved by the Board of Governors.

These traps illustrate the importance of distinguishing between formal rules, operational practice, and political dynamics across the institutions covered.

UN Security Council Reform: The “Uniting for Consensus” Proposal and the African Position

The debate over expanding the UN Security Council (UNSC) has produced two rival reform models since the 1990s. The G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan) advocates new permanent seats with veto power, while the “Uniting for Consensus” (UfC) group — led by Italy, Pakistan, Mexico, Egypt and others — opposes new permanent members and instead proposes a larger pool of non‑permanent seats with longer, renewable terms. The UfC model, formally tabled in 2005, calls for an increase from 15 to 25 members, adding ten non‑permanent seats elected for two‑year terms with the possibility of immediate re‑election, and a periodic review mechanism every 15 years.

African states, coordinated through the African Union’s Ezulwini Consensus (2005), demand two permanent seats with veto power and five additional non‑permanent seats, arguing that the continent’s 54 members are under‑represented in a body that authorises peacekeeping missions on African soil. The AU’s position has been reiterated in every General Assembly debate since 2005, most recently in the 2023 “Intergovernmental Negotiations” (IGN) session where the African Group submitted a joint text linking any reform to the “right to veto” for new permanent members. The UfC group, however, insists that the veto should not be extended, citing the risk of further paralysis.

The practical impact of these competing texts is visible in the IGN’s “framework document” of 2022, which lists five clusters — categories of membership, the veto, regional representation, size of an enlarged Council, and working methods — but leaves each cluster bracketed. No consensus has emerged on the “veto restraint” pledge (the 2015 French‑Mexican initiative) because permanent members (P5) treat it as voluntary. In 2024 the General Assembly adopted a procedural resolution (A/RES/78/XXX) that merely “takes note” of the IGN report, underscoring the deadlock. For aspirants, the key analytical point is that reform requires a two‑thirds majority in the General Assembly and ratification by two‑thirds of member states including all P5 — a constitutional hurdle that makes any model without P5 buy‑in effectively aspirational.

WTO E‑Commerce Moratorium: Extension Dynamics and Developing Country Concerns

Since the 1998 Ministerial Declaration, WTO members have agreed not to impose customs duties on electronic transmissions. The moratorium has been renewed at every subsequent Ministerial Conference (MC) — 1999, 2001, 2003, 2005, 2009, 2011, 2013, 2015, 2017, 2022 — typically by consensus. The 2022 MC12 in Geneva extended the moratorium until MC13 (scheduled for 2024) while launching a work programme to examine its scope, definition of “electronic transmissions”, and revenue implications for developing countries.

Developing members, notably India, South Africa, and the African Group, argue that the moratorium erodes tariff revenue at a time when digital trade grows faster than physical trade. UNCTAD estimates that potential tariff losses for developing economies could reach $10‑12 billion annually if the moratorium becomes permanent. In contrast, developed members (US, EU, Japan) contend that the moratorium provides certainty for cross‑border data flows and that any revenue loss is offset by gains in digital services exports.

The 2023 “Joint Statement Initiative on E‑Commerce” (JSI) — a plurilateral negotiation involving 86 members — has produced a draft text on customs duties that explicitly references the moratorium. However, the JSI text does not bind non‑participants, and the moratorium itself remains a Ministerial decision, not a covered agreement. At MC13 (February 2024, Abu Dhabi) the moratorium was extended again until MC14, with a decision to continue the work programme and to invite the Secretariat to prepare a factual report on revenue impact. The examiner often tests the distinction between a Ministerial decision (political, non‑justiciable) and a covered agreement (legally binding under the Dispute Settlement Understanding).

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The WTO e‑commerce moratorium is a legally binding obligation under the GATS.” State whether this is true or false and explain.
False. The moratorium is a Ministerial Decision, not a covered agreement. It is politically binding only for the period between Ministerial Conferences and can be discontinued by consensus at any MC. It does not create rights or obligations enforceable through the DSU.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “moratorium”, “Ministerial Decision”, or “plurilateral”, immediately classify the instrument: Ministerial Decision = non‑binding political commitment; Plurilateral Agreement = binding only on parties; Covered Agreement = binding on all members and subject to DSU. This classification eliminates half the answer choices.

IMF Surveillance under Article IV: The 2023 Integrated Policy Framework and Macro‑Critical Issues

Article IV of the IMF’s Articles of Agreement mandates bilateral surveillance — annual consultations with each member — and multilateral surveillance through the World Economic Outlook (WEO) and the Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR). In 2023 the Executive Board endorsed the Integrated Policy Framework (IPF), a systematic approach that combines monetary, fiscal, exchange‑rate, macroprudential, and capital‑flow management (CFM) tools to address macro‑critical risks such as sudden stops, currency substitution, and climate‑related transition shocks.

The IPF introduces a “policy matrix” that maps country‑specific vulnerabilities to a calibrated mix of instruments. For example, an emerging market with high foreign‑currency debt and limited reserves may be advised to combine a modest policy‑rate hike, targeted FX intervention, and temporary CFMs on outflows, while preserving fiscal space for social spending. The 2023 Guidance Note on Macro‑Critical Issues explicitly lists climate change, digitalisation, and income inequality as macro‑critical, meaning they must be addressed in Article IV reports even if they fall outside traditional macroeconomic variables.

Operationally, the 2023 Article IV consultation with Indonesia illustrated the IPF: staff recommended a tighter monetary stance, a gradual reduction of energy subsidies (fiscal), a flexible exchange rate, and the activation of the macroprudential buffer on property loans. The Board’s concluding statement (IMF Country Report No. 23/XXX) noted that the IPF “enhances the coherence of policy advice” but cautioned that CFMs should be “targeted, temporary, and transparent” to avoid protectionist perceptions. For examination purposes, remember that the IPF does not amend the Articles; it is a staff‑level analytical tool that guides the content of surveillance reports.

BRICS Expansion Criteria: The 2023 Johannesburg Summit and the New Membership Framework

The 15th BRICS Summit in Johannesburg (August 2023) admitted six new members — Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates — effective 1 January 2024. The summit communiqué established a two‑track membership framework: (1) “Full Members” with equal voting rights in the New Development Bank (NDB) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA); (2) “Partner Countries” that participate in selected working groups without financial commitments. The criteria for full membership, as articulated in the “BRICS Expansion Guidelines” annexed to the communiqué, are: (a) a sovereign state with a market‑oriented economy; (b) a GDP (PPP) exceeding $500 billion or a population above 50 million; (c) commitment to the BRICS Joint Statement on Reform of Multilateral Institutions; (d) willingness to contribute capital to the NDB in proportion to the existing capital key.

Argentina’s subsequent withdrawal (December 2023) before formal accession highlighted that the guidelines are not self‑executing; each candidate must complete a domestic ratification process and sign the NDB Agreement and CRA Treaty. The NDB’s capital key, revised in 2022, allocates shares based on GDP (PPP) and population, but the founding five retain a combined 55 % voting share. New members receive shares that dilute the founding members only after a capital increase approved by the Board of Governors — a step not yet taken as of mid‑2024.

The expansion also triggered a revision of the CRA’s swap lines: the total committed resources rose from $100 billion to $150 billion, with new members contributing 10 % of their quota. The 2024 BRICS Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Moscow confirmed that the CRA’s activation trigger — a “balance‑of‑payments need” certified by the IMF — remains unchanged, but the governance committee now includes a rotating chair from the expanded membership. Aspirants should note that BRICS decisions are consensus‑based; there is no weighted voting in the political pillar, unlike the NDB.

G20 Sustainable Finance Working Group: Taxonomy Alignment and Transition Finance Guidelines

Established under the 2021 Italian Presidency, the G20 Sustainable Finance Working Group (SFWG) produced the “G20 Sustainable Finance Roadmap” (2022) and, in 2023, the “Transition Finance Framework” endorsed by Finance Ministers in Gandhinagar. The framework defines “transition finance” as capital allocated to high‑emission sectors (steel, cement, chemicals, aviation) for credible decarbonisation pathways aligned with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5 °C goal. It sets three pillars: (i) a common taxonomy reference — the “G20 Taxonomy Alignment Principles” — that maps national taxonomies (EU Taxonomy, China Green Bond Catalogue, ASEAN Taxonomy) to a shared set of technical screening criteria; (ii) disclosure standards based on the ISSB’s IFRS S2 and the TCFD recommendations; (iii) a “transition label” for financial instruments that meet the criteria, verified by independent second‑party opinion providers.

The 2023 SFWG report notes that 18 G20 jurisdictions have published or are finalising national taxonomies. The Alignment Principles require that any taxonomy used for transition finance must (a) cover at least 80 % of sectoral emissions, (b) include a “do no significant harm” (DNSH) test for biodiversity and social safeguards, and (c) be subject to periodic review every three years. The framework also introduces a “transition risk metric” — the ratio of a firm’s capital expenditure on low‑carbon technologies to its total capex — to be disclosed in annual reports.

Implementation is voluntary; the G20 does not have legislative authority. However, the 2024 Brazilian Presidency has tasked the SFWG with developing a “G20 Transition Finance Dashboard” that aggregates taxonomy‑aligned flows reported by central banks and securities regulators. The dashboard will feed into the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) climate‑risk monitoring. For exam answers, distinguish between the G20’s political endorsement (non‑binding) and the binding nature of national regulations that adopt the taxonomy (e.g., the EU Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852).

  • Confusing the UfC proposal’s non‑permanent seat formula with the G4’s permanent‑seat demand; the UfC explicitly rejects new veto holders.
  • Treating the WTO e‑commerce moratorium as a covered agreement; it is a Ministerial Decision renewable by consensus.
  • Assuming the IMF’s Integrated Policy Framework amends the Articles of Agreement; it is a staff analytical tool, not a legal amendment.
  • Believing BRICS new members automatically receive equal voting power in the NDB; voting shares are re‑balanced only after a capital increase approved by the Board of Governors.
  • Thinking the G20 Transition Finance Framework creates a mandatory global taxonomy; it provides alignment principles that national authorities may adopt voluntarily.
  • Overlooking that the African Union’s Ezulwini Consensus links any UNSC reform to veto rights for new permanent members, a condition the P5 have not accepted.
  • Misreading the CRA’s activation trigger as a unilateral BRICS decision; it still requires an IMF‑certified balance‑of‑payments need.

The Quad: Institutional Evolution, Working Group Architecture, and Strategic Convergence in the Indo‑Pacific

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) originated in 2007 as a loose consultative mechanism among Australia, India, Japan, and the United States following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami relief coordination. The first iteration collapsed in 2008 after Australian withdrawal amid Chinese diplomatic pressure. The format was revived at the official level in November 2017 on the margins of the ASEAN Summit in Manila and elevated to the ministerial level in September 2019. The first Leaders' Summit was held virtually in March 2021, establishing a regular cadence of annual in‑person summits (Washington 2021, Tokyo 2022, Hiroshima 2023, Wilmington 2024). Unlike a treaty‑based alliance, the Quad has no secretariat, no standing military structure, and no collective defence clause; it operates through consensus‑based political commitments documented in joint statements and fact sheets.

The operational architecture rests on six standing working groups, each co‑led by two partners: (1) Climate Change (Australia‑India), (2) Critical and Emerging Technology (Japan‑US), (3) Cybersecurity (Australia‑Japan), (4) Health Security and Pandemic Preparedness (India‑US), (5) Infrastructure (Japan‑Australia), and (6) Maritime Domain Awareness (India‑US). Two additional coordination mechanisms — the Quad Senior Cyber Group and the Quad Space Working Group — report directly to the foreign ministers. The 2022 Tokyo Summit launched the Indo‑Pacific Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA) initiative, integrating commercial satellite radio‑frequency data, automatic identification system feeds, and synthetic‑aperture radar imagery to provide near‑real‑time maritime picture to partner nations in Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands. The 2023 Hiroshima Summit produced the Quad Principles on Technology Design, Development, Governance, and Use, a non‑binding normative framework covering semiconductors, AI, quantum, biotechnology, and 5G/6G, explicitly referencing "responsible innovation" and "trusted supply chains." The 2024 Wilmington Summit added a Quad Cancer Moonshot (cervical cancer elimination in the Indo‑Pacific), a Quad Ports of the Future Partnership (green shipping corridors), and a Quad STEM Fellowship programme. The Quad Vaccine Partnership (2021), which aimed to deliver 1.2 billion doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine manufactured by Biological E in India with US/Japan financing and Australian logistics, fell short of its target due to export restrictions and demand shifts but established a template for health‑security burden‑sharing. Examiners frequently test the distinction between the Quad's political character and AUKUS (a trilateral security pact with nuclear‑propulsion submarine technology transfer) or the Five Eyes (an intelligence‑sharing alliance with binding legal instruments). The Quad's value proposition lies in issue‑specific minilateralism that avoids the consensus paralysis of larger forums while remaining inclusive enough to avoid formal bloc‑formation rhetoric.

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation: Membership Expansion, Consensus Decision‑Making, and the Eurasian Security Architecture

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) was founded in June 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan, evolving from the "Shanghai Five" border‑demarcation talks (1996‑2001). The Charter, signed in 2002 and entering into force in 2003, enshrines consensus as the sole decision‑making rule — no weighted voting, no qualified majority. The Council of Heads of State (CHS) meets annually; the Council of Heads of Government (CHG) focuses on economic cooperation. The permanent Secretariat is in Beijing; the Regional Anti‑Terrorist Structure (RATS) Executive Committee sits in Tashkent. India and Pakistan acceded as full members in June 2017 after a six‑year observer‑to‑member process requiring ratification of the SCO Convention on Combating Terrorism, Separatism and Extremism (2001) and the SCO Drug Control Cooperation Programme. Iran's accession was finalised at the July 2023 New Delhi virtual summit (memorandum of obligations signed 2022, ratified 2023). Belarus signed the memorandum in 2022 and completed ratification in 2024, becoming the tenth member at the July 2024 Astana summit. Observer states (Afghanistan, Belarus until 2024, Mongolia) and dialogue partners (Turkey, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Nepal, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Maldives, UAE, Kuwait, Myanmar) expand the penumbra but lack voting rights.

The SCO's economic pillar remains under‑institutionalised relative to its security pillar. The SCO Development Bank and SCO Development Fund have been proposed since 2010 but stalled over capital‑key disagreements; the 2023 New Delhi summit reiterated "feasibility studies" without a launch timeline. The SCO Interbank Consortium (2006) and SCO Business Council (2006) facilitate trade finance in local currencies — a priority accelerated after 2022 sanctions on Russia. The 2022 Samarkand summit adopted the "SCO Economic Development Strategy 2030" targeting intra‑SCO trade growth, transport corridor harmonisation (notably the China‑Kyrgyzstan‑Uzbekistan railway), and digital economy cooperation. Energy cooperation focuses on the SCO Energy Club (2013) and the 2021 Agreement on Cooperation in the Field of Rational Use of Energy Resources. The security pillar centres on the "Three Evils" (terrorism, separatism, extremism) with RATS conducting joint exercises (e.g., "Pabbi‑Anti‑Terror" series) and maintaining a database of designated terrorist organisations. However, India‑Pakistan bilateral tensions prevent meaningful intelligence sharing on cross‑border terrorism; India has consistently blocked Pakistan‑linked listings in RATS. The 2024 Astana summit admitted Belarus, endorsed a "SCO Initiative on World Unity for Just Peace, Harmony and Development" (a Chinese‑drafted normative statement), and directed the Secretariat to draft a convention on countering the use of ICTs for terrorist purposes. For exam purposes, the SCO illustrates a China‑Russia anchored Eurasian grouping where consensus protects national vetoes, economic integration lags security coordination, and India's participation serves hedging rather than bandwagoning.

Examiner's Technique: Comparative Institutional Design
"Compare the decision‑making structures of the Quad and the SCO. How do their respective rules — consensus in the SCO versus voluntary coordination in the Quad — shape their ability to produce binding outcomes? Illustrate with one example from each grouping since 2022."
The SCO's Charter (Art. 6) mandates consensus for all decisions, giving each of the ten members a de facto veto. This ensures political cohesion but paralyses ambitious commitments: the SCO Development Bank has been "under study" since 2010 because Russia and China disagree on capital contributions and headquarters location. The 2023 New Delhi summit could not adopt a joint statement on the Ukraine conflict because India refused language condemning Russia, resulting in a Chair's Summary instead. The Quad has no charter, no secretariat, and no voting rule; outcomes are joint statements issued by leaders/ministers reflecting the lowest common denominator. This allows flexibility — the 2022 IPMDA launch and 2023 Technology Principles were produced without treaty ratification — but creates no legal obligation. The 2024 Quad Cancer Moonshot is a political pledge; partner countries may adjust contributions domestically without breach. In short, the SCO's consensus rule protects sovereignty at the cost of depth; the Quad's voluntarism enables speed and issue‑specific depth at the cost of enforceability. A strong answer contrasts the SCO's 2023 failure to issue a leaders' declaration on Ukraine with the Quad's 2023 Hiroshima Technology Principles — both outcomes of their respective decision architectures.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to "compare" two groupings, structure the answer in three layers: (1) legal basis (Charter vs. political declaration), (2) decision rule (consensus/veto vs. voluntary coordination), (3) empirical evidence of output (binding treaty vs. joint statement). Memorise one concrete post‑2022 example per grouping where the decision rule visibly determined the outcome — this converts abstract comparison into marked analysis.

The BBNJ Agreement: Treaty Negotiations, Marine Genetic Resources, and the Path to Entry into Force

The Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement) was adopted by consensus on 19 June 2023 at the resumed fifth session of the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC‑5.2) in New York, after nearly two decades of preparatory work (2004‑2017) and five formal negotiating sessions (2018‑2023). It opened for signature on 20 September 2023 and will enter into force 120 days after the 60th instrument of ratification or accession is deposited. As of mid‑2024, approximately 15 states have ratified (including Palau, Chile, Belize, Monaco, Seychelles, Micronesia, Mauritius, Bangladesh, Barbados, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Singapore, Spain, St. Lucia, and the European Union), with over 90 signatories. The Agreement addresses four substantive pillars in Part II‑V: (1) Marine Genetic Resources (MGR), including the fair and equitable sharing of benefits (Art. 7‑13); (2) Area‑Based Management Tools (ABMTs), including Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) (Art. 14‑26); (3) Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) for activities in areas beyond national jurisdiction (Art. 27‑39); and (4) Capacity Building and Transfer of Marine Technology (CB&TMT) (Art. 40‑51). A clearing‑house mechanism (Art. 52) will serve as the open‑access information platform for MGR data, MPA proposals, EIA reports, and capacity‑building opportunities.

The MGR benefit‑sharing regime (Art. 10‑11) distinguishes between monetary and non‑monetary benefits. Monetary benefits — triggered by commercialisation of MGR‑derived products — flow into a special fund administered by the Conference of Parties (COP), with allocation criteria to be developed by the COP's Finance Committee. Non‑monetary benefits include access to samples, digital sequence information (DSI), research collaboration, and technology transfer. The Agreement adopts a "notify‑and‑consult" approach for MGR collection: collectors must notify the clearing‑house but do not require prior consent, a compromise between the "common heritage of mankind" position (African Group, G77) and the "freedom of the high seas" position (industrialised fishing/biotech states). ABMTs/MPAs (Art. 17‑19) are proposed by parties, assessed by the Scientific and Technical Body (STB), and adopted by the COP by consensus; if consensus fails, a three‑quarters majority of parties present and voting applies — a rare voting provision in a UNCLOS‑implementing agreement. EIAs (Art. 28‑30) are required for planned activities that "may cause substantial pollution or significant and harmful changes" to the marine environment; the STB reviews screening and scoping reports, but the final authorisation remains with the flag State, subject to COP oversight. The COP (Art. 49) meets annually; the STB (Art. 50) comprises 15 experts elected for four‑year terms with equitable geographical distribution. The Agreement's relationship with existing bodies — the International Seabed Authority (ISA), Regional Fisheries Management Organisations (RFMOs), the International Maritime Organization (IMO) — is governed by "non‑undermining" clauses (Art. 4, 22) requiring coordination and avoidance of duplication. For exam answers, the BBNJ Agreement exemplifies the "package deal" negotiation method: nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, and the MGR benefit‑sharing / MPA voting / EIA flag‑State balance reflects the final political equilibrium.

The UN Convention against Corruption: The Implementation Review Mechanism, Asset Recovery Provisions, and the 2023 Conference of States Parties Outcomes

The United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC), adopted by the General Assembly on 31 October 2003 (Resolution 58/4) and entering into force on 14 December 2005, is the only universal anti‑corruption treaty with 190 parties as of July 2024. Its Implementation Review Mechanism (IRM), established by the Conference of States Parties (CoSP) Resolution 3/1 (2009), operates in five‑year cycles. The first cycle (2010‑2015) reviewed Chapters III (Criminalisation) and IV (International Cooperation); the second cycle (2015‑2020) covered Chapters II (Prevention) and V (Asset Recovery). The third cycle, launched at CoSP‑8 (2019) and running 2020‑2025, revisits Chapters III and IV with updated review guidelines (Resolution 8/1). Each State party undergoes peer review by two other parties (one from the same regional group, one from a different group) based on a comprehensive self‑assessment checklist, followed by a country visit (optional but encouraged) and a draft executive summary. The final country review report and executive summary are published unless the reviewed State objects — a transparency improvement over the first cycle. As of CoSP‑10 (Atlanta, December 2023), 186 parties had completed first‑cycle reviews, 178 second‑cycle reviews, and 92 third‑cycle reviews.

Chapter V (Asset Recovery, Arts. 51‑58) is UNCAC's most innovative and politically sensitive chapter. Article 51 establishes asset recovery as a "fundamental principle"; Article 53 permits direct recovery of property through civil proceedings in the requested State; Article 55 allows the requested State to recognise foreign freezing/confiscation orders; Article 57 governs the return and disposal of confiscated assets, prioritising return to the requesting State or, where appropriate, to victims or a dedicated fund. The 2023 CoSP‑10 adopted Resolution 10/1 on "Strengthening asset recovery," urging parties to establish central authorities, use non‑conviction‑based confiscation, and adopt beneficial‑ownership registries. It also endorsed the "UNCAC Coalition" civil‑society parallel reporting framework. The CoSP‑10 further adopted Resolution 10/3 on "Private sector transparency," calling for mandatory beneficial‑ownership disclosure in public procurement and extractive industries, and Resolution 10/5 on "Non‑trial resolutions," encouraging safeguards (judicial oversight, transparency, victim compensation) for deferred prosecution agreements and settlement mechanisms. The next CoSP‑11 is scheduled for Doha, Qatar, in December 2025. For exam purposes, UNCAC illustrates how a universal treaty with a peer‑review mechanism can generate compliance pressure without sanctions, while asset recovery remains hampered by dual‑criminality requirements, banking secrecy, and political will — issues the IRM's country reports systematically document but cannot enforce.

The International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure: Governance Models, Funding Architecture, and Global South Leadership

The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was jointly launched by India and France at the 2015 Paris COP21. The ISA Framework Agreement opened for signature in November 2016 at COP22 Marrakech, entered into force on 6 December 2017 after 15 ratifications, and as of July 2024 has 116 signatories and 94 parties. Membership is open to all UN member states; the original "sunshine countries" criterion (between the Tropics) was removed by the 2020 Amendment to the Framework Agreement (adopted at the Third Assembly, 2020). The ISA Assembly (all parties) is the supreme decision‑making body, meeting annually; the Council (14 members elected for two‑year terms with equitable geographical representation) provides guidance between Assemblies. The Secretariat, headquartered in Gurugram, India, is led by a Director General appointed by the Assembly for a four‑year term. The ISA's programmatic portfolio comprises nine programmes: (1) Scaling Solar Applications for Agricultural Use, (2) Affordable Finance at Scale, (3) Solar for All (off‑grid), (4) Solar Parks, (5) Solar Rooftop, (6) Solar‑based Cold Chain, (7) Solar‑powered E‑Mobility, (8) Solar Hydrogen, and (9) Solar Waste Management. The "Affordable Finance at Scale" programme targets a $1 trillion solar investment mobilisation by 2030, leveraging the ISA's Solar Facility (a payment guarantee mechanism backed by a $35 million corpus from India and $10 million from the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet) and partnerships with MDBs. The ISA's budget is funded by voluntary contributions; India committed $27 million (2016‑2021) and hosts the Secretariat rent‑free.

The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) was launched by Prime Minister Modi at the 2019 UN Climate Action Summit. Its Charter was adopted at the First Governing Council Meeting (June 2022). As of July 2024, CDRI has 39 members: 31 countries (including G20 members, small island developing states, and African nations) and 8 organisations (UN agencies, MDBs, private sector networks). The Governing Council (all members) meets annually; the Executive Committee (12 members elected for two years) oversees operations. The Secretariat is in New Delhi, hosted by India. CDRI's work programme rests on three pillars: (1) Technical Assistance and Capacity Building (e.g., the Infrastructure Resilience Accelerator Fund for SIDS), (2) Knowledge Products and Standards (e.g., the Global Infrastructure Resilience Rating Framework, launched 2023), and (3) Advocacy and Partnerships (e.g., the International Conference on Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, ICDRI, annual since 2021). India committed $70 million (2019‑2024) as core funding; the UK, Australia, and the EU have contributed to specific programmes. CDRI does not finance projects directly but enables "resilience‑by‑design" through upstream advisory services. Both ISA and CDRI exemplify a new model of Global South‑led, issue‑specific multilateralism: treaty‑light (ISA) or charter‑based (CDRI), hosted by the initiating country, funded by voluntary contributions with a large anchor donor, and focused on implementation pipelines rather than norm‑setting. They complement — not substitute — the UNFCCC and Sendai Framework, and their governance avoids the consensus‑paralysis of universal bodies by limiting membership to willing participants.

  • Confusing the Quad's voluntary coordination with the SCO's consensus rule; the Quad produces joint statements without vetoes, the SCO requires consensus for any decision including declarations.
  • Assuming the BBNJ Agreement's MPA voting provision (three‑quarters majority) applies to all its pillars; it applies only to ABMT/MPA adoption when consensus fails, not to MGR benefit‑sharing or EIA authorisation.
  • Treating UNCAC's Implementation Review Mechanism as a sanctioning body; it produces country reports and executive summaries but has no enforcement power — compliance is political, not judicial.
  • Believing ISA membership is restricted to tropical countries; the 2020 Amendment removed the geographic criterion, making ISA universal.
  • Assuming CDRI directly finances resilient infrastructure projects; it provides technical assistance, standards, and advisory services, not project finance.
  • Overlooking that the SCO's economic initiatives (Development Bank, Development Fund) remain unimplemented after 14 years due to capital‑key disagreements, while its security pillar (RATS) conducts regular exercises.
  • Misreading the Quad's IPMDA as a military surveillance system; it fuses commercial satellite data for maritime awareness and is shared with partner nations, not a classified intelligence platform.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to analyse institutional design choices, negotiation trade‑offs, and implementation gaps across the evolving landscape of minilateral, regional, and treaty‑based governance.

UNFCCC Global Stocktake: Design, First Cycle Outcomes, and Implications for NDC Ambition

The Global Stocktake (GST) is the centrepiece of the Paris Agreement’s “ratchet mechanism”, mandated under Article 14 to assess collective progress toward the Agreement’s long‑term goals every five years. The first GST cycle ran from 2021 to 2023 and concluded at COP28 in Dubai with Decision 1/CMA.5, known as the “UAE Consensus”. The process is structured in three phases: (1) information collection and preparation, where Parties, the UNFCCC secretariat, and non‑state actors submit synthesis reports on mitigation, adaptation, and means of implementation; (2) technical assessment, conducted by the Technical Dialogue under the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) and the Subsidiary Body for Implementation (SBI); and (3) consideration of outputs, where the Conference of the Parties serving as the Meeting of the Parties to the Paris Agreement (CMA) adopts a political decision that informs the next round of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) due in 2025.

The first GST’s technical findings highlighted a significant “emissions gap”: aggregate NDCs would lead to a 2.5–2.9 °C temperature rise by 2100, far above the 1.5 °C limit. On adaptation, the stocktake noted that only 40 % of Parties had submitted adaptation communications, and finance flows remained well below the $100 bn per year goal. The political decision at COP28 called for “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in a just, orderly and equitable manner”, the first explicit reference to fossil‑fuel phase‑down in a UNFCCC outcome. It also urged Parties to align their next NDCs with 1.5 °C pathways, enhance adaptation planning, and scale up climate finance, including the operationalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund.

For aspirants, the GST is a test case of how procedural design (technical dialogue, consensus‑based political decision) shapes substantive ambition. The next GST (2026‑2028) will evaluate the 2025 NDCs and the implementation of the UAE Consensus, making it a recurring anchor for climate‑policy analysis in GS II.

UNCLOS Part XV Dispute Settlement: Compulsory Procedures, Exceptions, and ITLOS Jurisprudence

Part XV of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) establishes a compulsory, binding dispute‑settlement system for all States Parties. Section 1 requires parties to settle disputes peacefully; Section 2 provides that, failing settlement, any party may unilaterally submit the dispute to one of four forums: the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the International Court of Justice (ICJ), an arbitral tribunal constituted under Annex VII, or a special arbitral tribunal under Annex VIII for specific technical matters. The default forum, if parties have not made a declaration choosing a specific body, is Annex VII arbitration.

Article 298 allows States to opt out of compulsory procedures for three categories: (i) disputes concerning maritime boundary delimitation or historic bays/titles; (ii) disputes involving military activities; and (iii) disputes concerning law enforcement activities in the exclusive economic zone. As of 2024, over 40 States have lodged such declarations, notably China (2006) on maritime delimitation and military activities, and the United States (non‑party) which relies on customary law. The opt‑out does not affect the jurisdiction of ITLOS for prompt release of vessels (Article 292) or provisional measures (Article 290).

ITLOS jurisprudence illustrates the system’s reach. In the Arctic Sunrise case (Netherlands v. Russia, 2015), the Tribunal ordered Russia to release the vessel and crew, affirming flag‑State jurisdiction and the right to peaceful protest in the EEZ. In the South China Sea Arbitration (Philippines v. China, 2016), an Annex VII tribunal ruled on the legal status of features and the invalidity of China’s “nine‑dash line”, though China refused to participate. The Enrica Lexie case (Italy v. India, 2020) saw ITLOS grant provisional measures for the release of Italian marines, later resolved through a bilateral agreement. These cases demonstrate that even with opt‑outs, the compulsory framework generates authoritative legal findings that shape State behaviour and scholarly discourse.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “Which of the following disputes is NOT subject to compulsory settlement under UNCLOS Part XV if a State has filed an Article 298 declaration? (a) Delimitation of the continental shelf beyond 200 nm; (b) Prompt release of a detained vessel; (c) Law enforcement against illegal fishing in the EEZ; (d) Interpretation of Article 76 on the continental shelf.”
Correct answer: (c). Article 298(1)(b) permits exclusion of disputes concerning law enforcement activities in the EEZ. Prompt release (Article 292) and provisional measures (Article 290) are expressly excluded from opt‑outs. Delimitation disputes (a) are excludable under Article 298(1)(a), but the question asks for the one NOT subject to compulsory settlement if a declaration is filed; law‑enforcement disputes are excludable, while prompt release is never excludable. Hence (c) is the dispute that a State can remove from compulsory jurisdiction.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the three Article 298 opt‑out categories and the two non‑excludable procedures (prompt release, provisional measures). In MCQs, the phrase “notwithstanding any declaration under Article 298” signals a non‑excludable matter. For descriptive answers, cite the Arctic Sunrise and Enrica Lexie cases to show how ITLOS applies these rules in practice.

G20 Health Working Group: Architecture, Pandemic Preparedness, and the 2023 Delhi Declaration

The G20 Health Working Group (HWG) was institutionalised during the 2017 German presidency to coordinate health‑policy responses across the world’s major economies. It reports to the G20 Finance and Health Ministers’ Meetings and operates through three thematic tracks: (1) health‑system resilience and universal health coverage; (2) pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response (PPPR); and (3) digital health and antimicrobial resistance. The HWG’s secretariat rotates with the G20 presidency, while the World Health Organization (WHO) provides technical support and the World Bank contributes financing analytics.

Under the 2023 Indian presidency, the HWG produced the “Delhi Declaration on Health”, which committed G20 members to: (a) strengthen the International Health Regulations (IHR) 2005 through a targeted amendment process concluded at the 2024 World Health Assembly; (b) establish a Global Pandemic Accord negotiation timeline aiming for adoption by 2025; (c) create a G20 Joint Finance‑Health Task Force to mobilise $10 bn annually for PPPR in low‑ and middle‑income countries; and (d) promote equitable access to medical countermeasures via the mRNA technology transfer hub in South Africa and the WHO Bio‑Hub. The declaration also endorsed the “One Health” approach, integrating human, animal, and environmental health surveillance.

Operationally, the HWG’s outputs are non‑binding political commitments. Their implementation relies on domestic budgetary processes, WHO governing‑body decisions, and the newly created Pandemic Fund (hosted by the World Bank, launched 2022). The 2024 Brazilian presidency has prioritised climate‑health linkages and the operationalisation of the Pandemic Fund’s first replenishment cycle. For GS II, the HWG exemplifies how a finance‑centric forum (G20) can legitimise health‑governance agendas that otherwise stall in the WHO’s consensus‑driven assembly.

IMF Conditionality Evolution: From Structural Adjustment to Country‑Owned Programs and the 2021 Conditionality Review

IMF conditionality — the policy measures a member must implement to access financial resources — has undergone three major paradigm shifts. The 1980s “structural adjustment” era imposed macro‑stabilisation (fiscal deficit cuts, devaluation) and liberalisation (trade, finance, privatisation) as uniform prescriptions, often criticised for social‑impact neglect. The 1999‑2005 Poverty Reduction and Growth Facility (PRGF) introduced Poverty Reduction Strategy Papers (PRSPs) drafted by borrowing countries with civil‑society participation, marking the first formal “country ownership” requirement.

The 2009 Flexible Credit Line (FCL) and 2011 Precautionary and Liquidity Line (PLL) created “qualification‑based” instruments for strong performers, where conditionality is ex‑ante (pre‑qualification criteria) rather than ex‑post (program‑specific measures). The 2021 Comprehensive Conditionality Review, endorsed by the Executive Board, codified four principles: (i) parity — conditions must be proportionate to the macro‑criticality of the problem; (ii) country ownership — design through national dialogue, not IMF‑drafted blueprints; (iii) transparency — publication of conditionality matrices; and (iv) adaptability — conditions can be modified as circumstances evolve, with streamlined waiver procedures.

Empirically, the 2022‑2023 lending surge (over $250 bn in new arrangements) saw a higher share of “policy‑based” lending (e.g., Resilience and Sustainability Trust) where climate‑reform conditions are linked to disbursement tranches. Critics argue that parity remains uneven: low‑income countries still face more structural benchmarks per dollar than emerging markets. The Review also mandated an independent evaluation every five years, the first due in 2026. Understanding this trajectory is essential for analysing IMF‑programme design questions in GS II.

World Bank Inspection Panel: Mandate, Case Law, and Accountability Gaps

Established in 1993 by a Board resolution, the Inspection Panel is the World Bank’s independent accountability mechanism. It receives requests for inspection from any group of two or more people who believe their rights or interests have been, or are likely to be, adversely affected by a Bank‑financed project. The Panel’s three‑member roster (appointed for five‑year terms) conducts eligibility screening, investigation, and issues a report with findings and recommendations to the Board, which then decides on a Management Action Plan.

Landmark cases illustrate its reach. The Chad‑Cameroon Pipeline (2000) investigation found failures in environmental assessment and indigenous‑people consultation, leading to a revised safeguard framework. The Narmada Dam (India, 2000) request resulted in the Panel’s first “non‑registration” decision, citing insufficient evidence of direct harm — a precedent criticised for narrowing standing. The Mongolia: Mining (2017) case upheld complaints on inadequate resettlement planning, prompting the Bank to adopt the 2018 Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) with stronger Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) requirements.

Despite these successes, structural gaps persist. The Panel cannot award compensation; remedies are limited to project redesign or mitigation measures. Its jurisdiction excludes International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) projects, which have separate accountability offices (CAO and MIGA’s Compliance Advisor Ombudsman). Moreover, the Board’s political composition often delays or dilutes Management Action Plans. The 2023 Independent Evaluation Group review recommended expanding the Panel’s mandate to include retrospective reviews of closed projects and a formal follow‑up mechanism — proposals still under Board consideration.

  • Confusing the Global Stocktake’s political decision with a legally binding target; the GST outcome is a consensus‑based guidance, not a treaty obligation.
  • Assuming Article 298 opt‑outs remove all maritime disputes from compulsory settlement; prompt release and provisional measures remain compulsory regardless of declarations.
  • Treating G20 Health Working Group declarations as enforceable commitments; they are political statements that require domestic legislation and WHO assembly action to become binding.
  • Believing IMF conditionality under the 2021 Review eliminates structural benchmarks; parity and country ownership reduce but do not remove macro‑critical structural conditions.
  • Thinking the World Bank Inspection Panel can order financial compensation; it only recommends project‑level remedies, and the Board controls implementation.
  • Overlooking that the Inspection Panel’s jurisdiction excludes IFC and MIGA projects, which have separate accountability mechanisms.
  • Misreading the “UAE Consensus” as a fossil‑fuel phase‑out mandate; the text calls for “transitioning away” in a just, orderly manner, leaving timing to national circumstances.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to dissect institutional design choices, negotiation trade‑offs, and implementation gaps across the evolving landscape of minilateral, regional, and treaty‑based governance.

UN Peacekeeping Financing and the Scale of Assessments

The financial architecture of UN peacekeeping rests on a system of assessed contributions that differs from the regular budget scale. The General Assembly, acting on the recommendation of the Committee on Contributions, adopts a peacekeeping scale every three years. The scale is derived from the regular budget capacity‑to‑pay methodology but applies a series of discounts for developing countries and a surcharge for the five permanent members of the Security Council, reflecting their special responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. For the 2022‑2024 period the top contributors are the United States (27.89 %), China (15.21 %), Japan (8.56 %), Germany (6.09 %), the United Kingdom (5.79 %) and France (5.61 %). The discounts reduce the assessed share of least‑developed countries to a floor of 0.001 % while the surcharge adds 5 % to the permanent members’ regular budget rates. The scale is applied to the approved peacekeeping budget, which for 2023‑2024 stands at approximately $6.4 billion across twelve active missions.

Contributions are due in two equal instalments each year. Late payments trigger the “cash‑flow” mechanism: the Secretariat may delay reimbursements to troop‑ and police‑contributing countries (TCCs/PCCs) until sufficient cash is available. This creates a feedback loop where chronic arrears by major contributors — notably the United States, which has accumulated arrears exceeding $1 billion at various points — constrain the liquidity available for troop reimbursements, affecting mission readiness. The General Assembly has repeatedly urged members to pay in full and on time, and the 2021 “Peacekeeping Financing Reform” resolution (A/RES/75/292) introduced a “reserve fund” of $150 million, financed by voluntary contributions, to smooth short‑term cash gaps.

A distinct feature is the “troop‑cost reimbursement” system. TCCs/PCCs are reimbursed at standard rates set by the General Assembly (e.g., $1,428 per soldier per month for infantry, $1,800 for formed police units) plus a “contingent‑owned equipment” (COE) rate. These rates are reviewed every three years; the 2020 review increased infantry rates by 2.5 % to reflect inflation. Reimbursements are made in US dollars, exposing contributors to exchange‑rate risk. The Secretariat issues quarterly “financial performance reports” that track assessed contributions, payments received, and outstanding balances, providing transparency for the Fifth Committee’s oversight.

The interplay between the assessed scale, cash‑flow constraints, and reimbursement rates shapes mission planning. When cash shortfalls persist, the Department of Peace Operations may defer the deployment of new units or reduce the size of existing contingents, directly affecting mandate implementation. Understanding this financing chain is essential for analysing questions on peacekeeping sustainability, burden‑sharing debates, and the political dynamics of Security Council reform.

WTO Subsidies and Countervailing Measures: The SCM Agreement and Recent Jurisprudence

The Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (SCM Agreement) classifies subsidies into three categories: prohibited, actionable, and non‑actionable (the latter lapsed in 1999). Prohibited subsidies are those contingent upon export performance or upon the use of domestic over imported goods (Article 3). Actionable subsidies cause adverse effects to the interests of another Member — injury to a domestic industry, nullification or impairment of benefits, or serious prejudice (Article 5). The Agreement also sets out detailed rules for countervailing duty (CVD) investigations, requiring a determination of subsidy existence, specificity, and injury (Articles 10‑23).

Recent dispute‑settlement practice illustrates the evolving interpretation of “specificity” and “serious prejudice”. In United States — Countervailing Measures on Certain Products from China (DS543, 2022), the Appellate Body upheld the Panel’s finding that the US Department of Commerce’s “benefit‑to‑the‑recipient” methodology for calculating subsidy rates was inconsistent with Article 14(b) because it failed to use an appropriate market benchmark. The ruling reinforced the requirement that investigating authorities must rely on market‑based benchmarks available in the subsidising country, or, if unavailable, construct a benchmark using external data under strict conditions.

In European Union — Subsidies on Large Civil Aircraft (DS316, 2020), the Panel addressed “serious prejudice” arising from launch aid to Airbus. The Panel found that the EU’s repayable launch aid conferred a benefit because the loans were provided at below‑market rates, and that the aid caused serious prejudice by displacing US exports in third markets. The decision clarified that “displacement” can be demonstrated through econometric modelling of market share shifts, not merely through direct head‑to‑head competition.

Another notable development is the 2021 “Joint Statement Initiative on Subsidies” (JSI‑Subsidies), a plurilateral effort among 45 Members to negotiate disciplines on industrial subsidies, particularly those granted by state‑owned enterprises. While not yet concluded, the JSI‑Subsidies reflects a growing consensus that the existing SCM framework inadequately addresses non‑market economies’ pervasive subsidy practices. The initiative proposes a “transparency‑plus” mechanism: mandatory notification of all subsidies above a de‑minimis threshold, coupled with a “subsidy‑impact assessment” for subsidies deemed likely to cause serious prejudice.

For domestic CVD practitioners, the key procedural safeguard remains the “sunset review” (Article 21.3), which mandates termination of duties after five years unless a review demonstrates that expiry would lead to continuation or recurrence of subsidisation and injury. The 2023 US‑China CVD sunset reviews on solar cells and steel products illustrate how authorities must reassess subsidy margins using updated benchmarks, often resulting in reduced duty rates.

Examiner's Technique: Applying SCM Categories to a Fact Pattern
A developing country provides a 10 % tax credit to all manufacturers that export more than 30 % of their output. The credit is administered by the finance ministry and is not limited to specific enterprises or sectors. A trading partner initiates a CVD investigation. Classify the subsidy under the SCM Agreement and state whether it is prohibited, actionable, or non‑actionable.
The tax credit is contingent upon export performance (export share >30 %). Under Article 3.1(a) of the SCM Agreement, subsidies contingent upon export performance are prohibited per se, regardless of specificity. The fact that the credit is broadly available does not remove the export contingency. Therefore the measure is a prohibited subsidy. The investigating authority may recommend withdrawal of the subsidy or impose countervailing duties without needing to demonstrate injury.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to classify a subsidy, first check for export or import‑substitution contingency — that alone makes it prohibited. If no contingency, test for specificity (enterprise, industry, region). Only if specific does it become actionable; non‑specific subsidies are generally non‑actionable (though the non‑actionable category expired). Memorise the three‑step filter: contingency → specificity → adverse effects.

IMF Lending Facilities: The Flexible Credit Line, Precautionary and Liquidity Line, and the Short‑Term Liquidity Line

The IMF’s precautionary financing toolkit has expanded beyond the traditional Stand‑By Arrangement (SBA) to include three “qualification‑based” instruments that provide liquidity without ex‑post conditionality. The Flexible Credit Line (FCL), created in 2009 and refined in 2011, targets members with very strong policy frameworks and track records. Access is capped at 1000 % of quota (exceptionally higher in crises) and is available for one‑ or two‑year periods, renewable. Qualification is assessed annually by staff and approved by the Executive Board; once qualified, the member can draw at any time without further policy conditions. The FCL has been used by Colombia, Mexico, Poland, and Chile, with Colombia drawing $10.8 billion in 2020 during the pandemic.

The Precautionary and Liquidity Line (PLL), introduced in 2011, serves members with sound policies but some vulnerabilities that preclude FCL qualification. Access is limited to 500 % of quota (up to 1000 % in exceptional circumstances) for a six‑month initial period, extendable to one year. PLL arrangements include a limited set of “qualification‑maintenance” conditions — typically macro‑critical structural benchmarks — that are monitored semi‑annually. Morocco (2012, 2018) and North Macedonia (2021) have used the PLL.

The Short‑Term Liquidity Line (SLL), approved in 2022, addresses the need for rapid, unconditional liquidity for members with strong fundamentals facing temporary external shocks. The SLL provides up to 145 % of quota (capped at SDR 10 billion) for a 12‑month period, renewable once. Unlike the FCL and PLL, the SLL does not require a full qualification assessment; instead, eligibility is based on a “strong policy framework” indicator and a debt‑sustainability analysis. The SLL carries a lower interest rate (the SDR rate plus a margin) and no conditionality beyond the requirement to maintain the policy framework. As of early 2024, no member has yet drawn on the SLL, but several emerging‑market economies have expressed interest.

All three instruments share a common design principle: ex‑ante qualification replaces ex‑post conditionality, reducing stigma and enabling faster disbursement. The 2021 Comprehensive Conditionality Review endorsed this approach, noting that qualification‑based facilities improve crisis prevention. However, critics argue that the high access limits for the FCL concentrate IMF resources on a few large economies, while low‑income countries remain reliant on concessional facilities with extensive conditionality. The 2023 Review of the FCL and PLL recommended tightening the “very strong” policy benchmark for FCL entry and enhancing transparency of qualification assessments.

BRICS Payment System and De‑dollarisation Initiatives

Since the 2023 Johannesburg Summit, BRICS has accelerated work on a cross‑border payment infrastructure that reduces reliance on the US dollar and the SWIFT network. The centrepiece is “BRICS Pay”, a digital platform linking the national payment systems of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. The platform uses a distributed ledger to settle transactions in local currencies, with the New Development Bank (NDB) acting as settlement agent. A pilot launched in late 2023 processed over 2,000 transactions worth approximately $150 million in renminbi‑rupee and real‑ruble pairs.

Complementing BRICS Pay, the “BRICS Bridge” project explores interoperability with the Bank for International Settlements’ (BIS) Project mBridge, a multi‑central‑bank digital currency (CBDC) corridor involving the People’s Bank of China, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Bank of Thailand, and the Central Bank of the UAE. The BRICS Bridge aims to enable atomic settlement of wholesale CBDC transactions across the five BRICS central banks, leveraging the mBridge technical stack. The 2024 work plan targets a sandbox test by Q3 2024.

De‑dollarisation is also pursued through expanded use of local‑currency settlement frameworks in bilateral trade. The 2022 India‑Russia rupee‑ruble arrangement, the 2023 Brazil‑China yuan‑real settlement for soybeans, and the 2023 South Africa‑China rand‑yuan mechanism for mineral exports illustrate the trend. The NDB has issued its first local‑currency bonds — a 3‑year renminbi‑denominated bond (CNY 3 billion) in 2022 and a 5‑year rupee bond (INR 50 billion) in 2023 — to diversify its funding base and support project financing in member currencies.

Challenges remain. Capital account restrictions in several BRICS economies limit the free convertibility required for seamless cross‑border settlement. Legal harmonisation of payment‑system regulations, anti‑money‑laundering standards, and data‑localisation rules is at an early stage. Moreover, the geopolitical heterogeneity of the grouping — particularly the divergent strategic alignments of India and China — complicates consensus on governance of the payment infrastructure. The 2024 Kazan Summit is expected to adopt a “BRICS Payment Charter” outlining governance principles, dispute‑resolution mechanisms, and a roadmap for expanding membership to the six new invitees (Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE).

Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank: Governance, Capital Structure, and Project Portfolio

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) commenced operations in January 2016 with an authorised capital of $100 billion, of which $20 billion is paid‑in capital and $80 billion is callable. The Bank’s membership has grown to 106 approved members (as of 2024), comprising 57 regional and 49 non‑regional members. Voting power is allocated on a share‑based formula: each member receives basic votes (equal for all) plus additional votes proportional to its subscribed capital. China holds the largest share (26.6 % of total voting power), followed by India (7.6 %), Russia (6.0 %), Germany (4.2 %), and the United Kingdom (3.5 %). The Board of Governors, meeting annually, is the highest decision‑making body; the non‑resident Board of Directors (12 members) oversees operations and approves projects.

The AIIB’s governance model emphasises “lean” management: a small resident staff (approximately 300) and a project‑preparation facility that co‑finances with other multilateral development banks (MDBs). The Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), adopted in 2016 and updated in 2021, aligns with the World Bank’s ESF but includes a “country‑systems” approach that permits reliance on borrower safeguards where they meet international standards. The AIIB also operates a “Project‑Level Accountability Mechanism” (PLAM) modelled on the World Bank Inspection Panel, though its jurisdiction covers only sovereign‑backed projects.

As of end‑2023, the AIIB’s approved project portfolio exceeds $40 billion across 200 projects. Sectoral distribution: energy (35 %), transport (30 %), water and sanitation (15 %), urban development (10 %), and digital infrastructure (10 %). Notable projects include the 2,400 MW Bhola‑II combined‑cycle power plant in Bangladesh (co‑financed with the World Bank), the Jakarta‑Bandung high‑speed rail in Indonesia (co‑financed with the Asian Development Bank), and the Trans‑Anatolian Natural Gas Pipeline (TANAP) in Turkey. The Bank has also pioneered “green bonds” — issuing its first $1 billion green bond in 2020, followed by a $2 billion sustainability bond in 2022, with proceeds earmarked for climate‑mitigation and adaptation projects.

The AIIB’s capital adequacy framework follows Basel‑III‑inspired risk‑weighted asset ratios, maintaining a capital‑to‑risk‑weighted‑assets ratio above 30 %, well above the 15 % regulatory minimum. The Bank’s credit ratings (AAA from S&P, Moody’s, and Fitch) reflect strong shareholder support, prudent risk management, and a high proportion of callable capital from highly rated members. The 2023 Corporate Strategy (2024‑2028) sets a target of $10 billion annual lending, with at least 50 % of new financing directed to climate‑finance activities, and a commitment to expand private‑sector mobilisation through the “AIIB Private Sector Window” launched in 2022.

  • Confusing the peacekeeping assessed scale with the regular budget scale; the peacekeeping scale includes permanent‑member surcharges and developing‑country discounts that do not apply to the regular budget.
  • Assuming all subsidies contingent on export performance are actionable; they are prohibited per se under Article 3.1(a) of the SCM Agreement.
  • Believing the FCL, PLL, and SLL carry identical conditionality; only the PLL includes qualification‑maintenance benchmarks, while the FCL and SLL are essentially conditionality‑free once qualified.
  • Thinking BRICS Pay is a single currency; it is a settlement platform that operates in multiple local currencies without a common BRICS currency.
  • Overlooking that AIIB voting power is not solely based on capital subscription; basic votes ensure every member has a minimum voice regardless of share size.
  • Treating the AIIB’s Project‑Level Accountability Mechanism as having the same mandate as the World Bank Inspection Panel; the PLAM covers only sovereign‑backed projects and lacks the power to award compensation.
  • Misreading the “BRICS Bridge” as a replacement for SWIFT; it is a wholesale CBDC interoperability experiment, not a retail messaging system.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to dissect institutional design choices, negotiation trade‑offs, and implementation gaps across the evolving landscape of minilateral, regional, and treaty‑based governance.

UN General Assembly Revitalization: Working Methods, Resolution Adoption, and the “Uniting for Peace” Mechanism

The General Assembly (GA) remains the only universal forum where all 193 Member States have equal voice. Since the 2005 World Summit, a series of resolutions — 60/1, 62/277 (2008), 69/313 (2015) and 75/1 (2020) — have sought to revitalize its work by strengthening the role of the President, streamlining the agenda, and encouraging interactive debates. The President of the GA, elected annually, now convenes high‑level thematic debates, appoints facilitators for contentious items, and oversees the “General Committee” that allocates items to the six Main Committees. Resolutions are adopted either by consensus (preferred for political declarations) or by recorded vote; the latter requires a two‑thirds majority for “important questions” (budget, admission of members, suspension of rights) under Article 18 of the Charter.

A distinctive tool is the “Uniting for Peace” resolution (377 (V), 1950), which empowers the GA to consider matters of international peace and security when the Security Council is deadlocked by a veto. The mechanism has been invoked ten times, most recently in 2022 (ES‑11/1) to address the Ukraine crisis, leading to the establishment of an independent commission of inquiry. The GA’s emergency special sessions (ESS) operate under a truncated procedural rule: a two‑thirds majority of members present and voting suffices, and the session can be convened within 24 hours of a request by nine Security Council members or a majority of GA members. While ESS resolutions are not legally binding, they carry significant political weight and have been used to authorize collective measures such as the 1956 Suez ceasefire and the 1980 Afghanistan condemnation.

Recent reform debates focus on three fronts: (1) reducing the number of repetitive resolutions by clustering thematic items; (2) enhancing the transparency of informal consultations through web‑casting and documentation; and (3) institutionalizing the “President’s Advisory Group” to ensure continuity across sessions. The 2023 “Pact for the Future” negotiations (mandated by resolution 76/307) aim to embed these working‑method improvements into a permanent framework, linking GA revitalization with Security Council reform and the 2030 Agenda review cycle.

IMF Quota Formula Review: The 16th General Review, Dynamic Quota Formula, and Emerging‑Market Representation

The IMF’s quota system determines each member’s financial contribution, voting power, and access to financing. The 15th General Review of Quotas, concluded in 2010 and effective 2016, doubled total quotas to SDR 477 billion and shifted 6.3 % of quota shares to dynamic emerging‑market and developing countries (EMDCs). The 16th General Review was launched in 2020 with a deadline of 2023, later extended to 2025, reflecting the difficulty of reaching consensus on a new quota formula.

The current quota formula (2008) blends four variables: GDP (weight 0.50), openness (0.30), economic variability (0.15), and international reserves (0.05). GDP is measured using a blend of market‑exchange‑rate (60 %) and purchasing‑power‑parity (40 %) conversions. The 16th Review debates centre on three issues: (i) increasing the PPP weight to better reflect the economic size of large developing economies; (ii) introducing a “compression factor” to limit the share of the largest advanced economies; and (iii) adjusting the variability and openness coefficients to reduce volatility in quota shares. The United States, holding 16.5 % of quotas and an effective veto (15 % threshold for major decisions), insists on preserving its blocking minority, while China, India, Brazil, and the African Group push for a larger collective share.

In 2023 the IMF’s Executive Board agreed on a “guiding principles” document that reaffirms the quota formula as the primary basis for share allocation, commits to protecting the voice of the poorest members, and mandates a comprehensive review of the formula’s variables by the 2025 Spring Meetings. Parallel to the quota review, the 2021 SDR allocation of SDR 650 billion (the largest in history) and the subsequent voluntary reallocation of SDR 100 billion to vulnerable countries via the Resilience and Sustainability Trust have provided temporary liquidity without altering quota shares. The outcome of the 16th Review will shape the Fund’s legitimacy and its capacity to respond to climate‑related balance‑of‑payments needs.

Examiner’s Technique: Comparative Quota‑Shift Calculation
A question asks: “If the 16th Review adopts a 70 % PPP / 30 % market‑rate GDP blend and applies a compression factor of 0.95 to the top five quota holders, estimate the directional change in China’s quota share relative to the 15th Review outcome (6.4 %). Explain the reasoning without performing exact arithmetic.”
China’s GDP at PPP is roughly 1.3 times its market‑rate GDP. Raising the PPP weight from 40 % to 70 % increases the GDP component of its quota formula by about (0.70‑0.40)×0.30 ≈ 9 % of the total formula weight. The compression factor of 0.95 reduces the shares of the top five (US, Japan, Germany, France, UK) by 5 %, redistributing that 5 % proportionally among all other members. China, as the largest non‑top‑five beneficiary, gains both from the higher PPP weight and from the redistributed compression pool. Therefore, China’s quota share would rise above 6.4 %, likely moving into the 7‑8 % range, while the US share would fall below its current 16.5 % but remain above the 15 % veto threshold.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a quota‑review question appears, first identify which review (15th vs 16th) and which formula variable is being altered. Sketch a quick table of the four variables and their weights; then note the political constraints (US veto, compression factor). Directional reasoning earns full marks even if precise numbers are not required.

WTO Ministerial Conference 12 (2022) Outcomes: Fisheries Subsidies, TRIPS Waiver, E‑Commerce Moratorium, and the Reform Agenda

The 12th Ministerial Conference (MC12) convened in Geneva from 12‑17 June 2022 after a four‑year hiatus caused by the COVID‑19 pandemic. It produced a package of decisions that addressed long‑standing negotiating deadlocks. The Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (WT/MIN(22)/2) prohibits subsidies for illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, for overfished stocks, and for fishing on the unregulated high seas. A transition period of two years for developing members and a “special and differential treatment” (S&DT) clause for least‑developed countries (LDCs) were included. The agreement enters into force once two‑thirds of members ratify; as of early 2024, 78 members have deposited instruments of acceptance.

On intellectual property, ministers adopted a decision (WT/MIN(22)/3) extending the TRIPS waiver for COVID‑19 vaccines — originally agreed at MC11 (2021) — to cover diagnostics and therapeutics for a period of five years. The waiver applies only to eligible developing members that have notified the WTO of insufficient manufacturing capacity. The decision also mandates a review after three years to assess implementation.

The moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, in place since 1998, was extended until MC13 (scheduled for 2024) with a commitment to intensify work on its scope, definition, and impact on developing‑country revenue. A dedicated work programme on WTO reform was launched, focusing on dispute‑settlement restoration, transparency notifications, and the integration of plurilateral Joint Statement Initiatives (JSIs) into the multilateral framework. The conference also adopted a declaration on food security, urging members to refrain from export restrictions on humanitarian food purchases by the World Food Programme.

MC12’s outcomes illustrate a shift toward “variable geometry” — binding agreements on specific sectors (fisheries) alongside flexible, time‑bound waivers (TRIPS) and moratorium extensions — reflecting the difficulty of achieving consensus across 164 members on comprehensive new rules.

G20 Finance Track: The Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion, BEPS Two‑Pillar Implementation, and the 2023 Delhi Summit Deliverables

The G20 Finance Track, comprising Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors, operates through a structured agenda of working groups. The Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion (GPFI), established in 2010, coordinates the G20’s financial‑inclusion action plan, monitors the G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators, and supports the implementation of the 2020 G20 Policy Guide on Digital Financial Inclusion. At the 2023 Delhi Summit, the GPFI reported that 1.2 billion adults gained access to formal financial services between 2011 and 2022, driven largely by mobile‑money platforms in Sub‑Saharan Africa and South Asia.

On international taxation, the G20 endorsed the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework’s Two‑Pillar Solution. Pillar One (Amount A) reallocates a portion of residual profits of the largest and most profitable multinational enterprises (MNEs) to market jurisdictions, with a revenue threshold of €20 billion and a profitability threshold of 10 %. Pillar Two introduces a global minimum corporate tax of 15 % through a coordinated set of rules: the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), the Undertaxed Payments Rule (UTPR), and the Subject‑to‑Tax Rule (STTR). The 2023 Delhi Communiqué confirmed that 138 jurisdictions representing more than 90 % of global GDP had committed to the framework, and urged swift domestic ratification of the Multilateral Convention (MLC) to implement Amount A by 2025.

The Finance Track also advanced work on crypto‑asset regulation, adopting the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) high‑level recommendations for the regulation, supervision, and oversight of crypto‑asset activities and markets. A G20‑level “Crypto‑Asset Reporting Framework” (CARF) was endorsed, requiring automatic exchange of information on crypto‑asset transactions between tax authorities from 2027. Additionally, the 2023 summit launched the “G20 Sustainable Finance Roadmap” to align financial flows with the Paris Agreement, mandating the development of transition‑finance taxonomies and the scaling of blended‑finance facilities for climate‑resilient infrastructure in emerging markets.

International Criminal Court: The Crime of Aggression – Activation, Jurisdictional Triggers, and the 2023 Review Conference Decisions

The crime of aggression was defined in the 2010 Kampala amendments to the Rome Statute. Activation required 30 ratifications and a decision by the Assembly of States Parties (ASP) after 1 January 2017. Both conditions were met: the 30th ratification (by Palestine) was deposited in 2017, and the ASP activated the jurisdiction on 15 December 2017, effective 17 July 2018. The crime covers the planning, preparation, initiation, or execution of an act of aggression by a person in a leadership position, where the act constitutes a manifest violation of the UN Charter.

Jurisdiction can be triggered in three ways: (1) a State Party referral; (2) a UN Security Council referral under Article 13(b); (3) the Prosecutor acting proprio motu with Pre‑Trial Chamber authorization. Crucially, the Court may exercise jurisdiction only over nationals of States Parties that have ratified the Kampala amendments, unless the Security Council refers a situation involving a non‑State Party. States Parties may opt out by lodging a declaration under Article 15‑bis(4); as of 2024, 43 States Parties have ratified, and 12 have opted out.

The 2023 Review Conference (held in The Hague) adopted a resolution reaffirming the Court’s jurisdiction over aggression, urging universal ratification of the Kampala amendments, and calling for the development of a “complementarity‑plus” framework to encourage national prosecutions. The Conference also mandated the Prosecutor to issue a policy paper on the investigation of aggression crimes, including the evidentiary threshold for “manifest violation” and the role of the UN General Assembly’s “Definition of Aggression” (Resolution 3314). No aggression case has yet reached trial; the Office of the Prosecutor has opened preliminary examinations in two situations (Ukraine and Palestine) but has not sought authorization to investigate, citing the high political sensitivity and the need for a clear Security Council or State Party referral.

  • Confusing the GA’s “Uniting for Peace” emergency special sessions with Security Council enforcement actions; ESS resolutions are recommendatory, not binding under Chapter VII.
  • Assuming the 16th IMF quota review has already concluded; the review is ongoing with a 2025 deadline and no new quota shares have been implemented.
  • Treating the MC12 fisheries subsidies agreement as fully in force; it requires two‑thirds ratification and, as of early 2024, has not yet entered into force.
  • Believing the G20’s Two‑Pillar tax solution is automatically binding; implementation depends on domestic legislation and the Multilateral Convention’s entry into force.
  • Thinking the ICC can prosecute aggression by any state; jurisdiction is limited to States Parties that have ratified the Kampala amendments unless the Security Council refers a non‑party situation.
  • Overlooking that the GA President’s advisory group is informal and lacks decision‑making authority; it only advises on agenda‑setting and working‑method improvements.
  • Assuming the IMF’s compression factor applies to all members; it targets only the top five quota holders to redistribute shares.

UN Peacebuilding Architecture: Peacebuilding Commission, Fund, and the 2020 Review

The United Nations peacebuilding architecture rests on three pillars created by the 2005 World Summit Outcome: the Peacebuilding Commission (PBC), the Peacebuilding Fund (PBF), and the Peacebuilding Support Office (PBSO).
