To mitigate these delays, the Secretariat introduced the “Fast‑Track Deployment” protocol in early 2024, which allows pre‑validated units with a PCRS composite score above 80 to bypass the standard 90‑day readiness verification and deploy within 30 days.

Financing of the PCRS and ITS is drawn from the peacekeeping support account, which is assessed separately from the regular peacekeeping budget. The 2023‑2024 support account allocation for PCRS operations was US$12.4 million, covering the portal maintenance, assessment missions, and ITS training delivery. The General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, in its 2024 session, endorsed a modest increase to US$14.1 million for the 2024‑2025 period to fund the expansion of the Fast‑Track protocol and the development of a real‑time equipment tracking dashboard.

Looking ahead, the 2026 assessment cycle will incorporate a new “environmental sustainability” pillar, reflecting the 2023 UN Climate Change Conference (COP28) call for peacekeeping missions to reduce their carbon footprint. The pillar will measure fuel efficiency of vehicle fleets, solar‑power adoption in camps, and waste‑management compliance, with a target composite score of 70 by 2028.

The International Monetary Fund's Food Shock Window: Design, Eligibility Criteria, and First Activations in 2023‑2024

The IMF established the Food Shock Window (FSW) in April 2022 as a temporary financing instrument under the Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) and the Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) to address acute food insecurity exacerbated by the COVID‑19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and climate‑driven supply disruptions. The window allows eligible low‑income and lower‑middle‑income members to access up to 50 % of quota (capped at SDR 1 billion) without a full‑fledged programme, provided they demonstrate a sharp deterioration in food‑security indicators — such as a 15 % rise in the domestic food price index or a 20 % increase in the number of people classified in IPC Phase 3 or above — within the preceding six months.

Eligibility is restricted to countries with an existing IMF‑supported arrangement (Extended Credit Facility, Stand‑By Arrangement, or a precautionary facility) or those that have requested a new RCF/RFI. The FSW does not impose structural conditionality; instead, it requires a “food‑security policy statement” outlining immediate measures to protect vulnerable populations, such as targeted cash transfers, strategic grain reserve releases, and removal of export restrictions on staple foods. The policy statement is reviewed by the IMF’s Strategy, Policy, and Review Department and must be endorsed by the Executive Board before disbursement.

The first activation occurred in June 2023 when Somalia accessed SDR 210 million (approximately US$280 million) under the RCF‑FSW to finance emergency food imports and scale up nutrition programmes in drought‑affected regions. A second activation followed in September 2023 for Yemen, which drew SDR 350 million under the RFI‑FSW to support the World Food Programme’s pipeline and to fund a temporary wheat‑flour subsidy. Both cases were processed under the “expedited” 30‑day approval track, reflecting the window’s design for rapid response. As of March 2024, the FSW had been utilized by six countries — Somalia, Yemen, Afghanistan, Haiti, South Sudan, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo — totalling SDR 1.42 billion in disbursements.

The window’s temporary nature is set to expire in April 2025 unless the Executive Board decides to extend it. The 2023 IMF Conditionality Review recommended that the FSW be integrated into a permanent “Food Security Facility” with a standing quota‑based access line, arguing that the ad‑hoc nature of the window creates uncertainty for donors and recipient governments alike. The review also highlighted the need for better data coordination with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) to standardize the food‑security triggers across regions.

Critics note that the FSW’s reliance on existing IMF programmes excludes several fragile states that lack an active arrangement, notably several Sahel countries facing simultaneous conflict and climate shocks. The 2024 Spring Meetings communiqué encouraged the Fund to explore a “stand‑alone” FSW track for non‑programme countries, subject to enhanced safeguards on governance and use‑of‑funds reporting.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "The IMF Food Shock Window can be accessed by any member country facing a food crisis, regardless of whether it has an IMF‑supported programme." True or False?
False. The FSW is only available to members that either have an existing IMF‑supported arrangement (ECF, SBA, precautionary facility) or are requesting a new RCF/RFI. Countries without any IMF programme cannot draw on the window unless the Executive Board creates a stand‑alone track, which as of 2024 has not been approved.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question references a new IMF financing window, first identify the facility (RCF vs RFI), the access limit (percentage of quota), and the eligibility gate (existing programme vs stand‑alone). The FSW is a classic “rapid‑access, low‑conditionality” tool — remember the 50 % of quota cap and the food‑security policy statement requirement.

The African Continental Free Trade Area Dispute Settlement Mechanism: Operationalization, Early Cases, and Cross‑Retaliation Provisions

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Agreement entered into force on 30 May 2019, and its Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) became operational in July 2020 after the adoption of the Dispute Settlement Rules and Procedures by the AfCFTA Council of Ministers. The DSB mirrors the WTO’s two‑tier structure: a panel stage and an appellate review stage, but the Appellate Body is not yet constituted; appeals are currently heard by a three‑member “Appeal Arbitration Panel” selected from a roster of African trade law experts.

As of December 2024, the DSB has constituted three panels. The first panel, established in March 2022, examined a rules‑of‑origin dispute concerning automotive components between Kenya and Tanzania; the panel issued its final report in November 2022, finding that Tanzania’s application of a 35 % regional value‑content threshold was inconsistent with the AfCFTA’s Annex 2 on Rules of Origin. The second panel, constituted in June 2023, addressed a services market‑access complaint by Egypt against a member state’s restrictions on cross‑border financial services; the panel’s report, circulated in February 2024, recommended the removal of the licensing barrier. The third panel, established in October 2024, is reviewing a dispute on non‑tariff measures affecting agricultural exports from Ghana.

A distinctive feature of the AfCFTA DSB is the explicit provision for cross‑retaliation across goods and services sectors (Article 23 of the Dispute Settlement Rules). Unlike the WTO, where cross‑retaliation requires a separate arbitration on the level of suspension, the AfCFTA rules allow the complainant to request suspension of concessions in a different sector if the respondent fails to comply within the reasonable period, subject to a proportionality test conducted by the original panel. This mechanism has not yet been invoked, but the 2022 Kenya‑Tanzania panel report included a provisional cross‑retaliation schedule should Tanzania not implement the ruling within 12 months.

The DSB’s operational budget is financed through the AfCFTA Secretariat’s regular budget, which is funded by assessed contributions from State Parties based on a scale of assessments approved by the Assembly of Heads of State and Government. The 2023‑2024 budget allocated US$3.2 million for dispute settlement activities, covering panelist fees, translation, and the maintenance of the electronic case‑management system (AfCFTA‑CMS). The Secretariat also provides technical assistance to State Parties on drafting panel requests and preparing written submissions, with a dedicated “Dispute Settlement Support Unit” established in 2021.

Challenges remain: the Appellate Body roster is still being populated, and the absence of a standing appellate institution creates uncertainty about the finality of panel reports. Moreover, enforcement relies on political goodwill; the AfCFTA Agreement does not provide for automatic authorization of retaliation, and the Assembly must endorse any suspension of concessions. The 2023 AfCFTA Council of Ministers meeting urged the acceleration of Appellate Body appointments and the development of a compliance monitoring dashboard to track implementation of rulings.

The World Bank's Climate Change Action Plan 2021‑2025: Mainstreaming Climate into Country Partnership Frameworks and the 2023 Mid‑Term Review

The World Bank Group (WBG) launched its Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) 2021‑2025 in June 2021, committing to align 35 % of its financing with climate co‑benefits by FY2025 and to ensure that at least 50 % of International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and International Development Association (IDA) operations have a climate‑relevant component. The plan is organized around five strategic pillars: (1) integrating climate into Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs), (2) scaling up climate finance, (3) supporting transformative mitigation and adaptation projects, (4) enhancing climate‑related data and analytics, and (5) strengthening institutional capacity and partnerships.

Under pillar 1, the Bank introduced a mandatory “Climate Change Screening” tool for all new CPFs starting in FY2022. The tool requires country teams to assess climate risks and opportunities across macro‑fiscal, sectoral, and social dimensions, and to embed quantified climate targets — such as renewable‑energy capacity additions or climate‑smart agriculture hectares — into the CPF results framework. By the end of FY2023, 78 % of active CPFs (62 out of 79) had completed the screening, and 45 % had incorporated at least one measurable climate indicator.

The 2023 Mid‑Term Review (MTR), presented to the Development Committee in October 2023, reported that climate‑related financing reached US$31.7 billion in FY2023, representing 38 % of total WBG commitments, surpassing the 35 % trajectory. The review highlighted two flagship programmes: the “Scaling Solar” initiative, which has mobilized over 5 GW of solar capacity across 12 countries since 2021, and the “Forest Landscape Restoration” programme, which has leveraged US$2.4 billion for restoration of 12 million hectares. However, the MTR also identified gaps: adaptation finance remains at only 12 % of climate finance, well below the 50 % target set for 2025, and the share of private‑sector mobilization through the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) has stagnated at around 18 % of total climate finance.

To address the adaptation shortfall, the Bank announced the “Adaptation Accelerator” in December 2023, a US$2 billion trust fund financed by donor contributions and IDA reflows, designed to de‑risk adaptation projects in low‑income countries through blended finance structures. The MTR also recommended strengthening the “Climate Change Knowledge Portal” to provide real‑time climate‑risk data for project appraisal, and expanding the “Country Climate and Development Reports” (CCDRs) to all IDA‑eligible countries by FY2025.

Governance of the CCAP is overseen by the Climate Change Steering Committee, chaired by the Managing Director of Operations, with representation from IBRD, IDA, IFC, and MIGA. The Committee reports annually to the Board of Executive Directors. The next comprehensive review is scheduled for 2025, coinciding with the end of the CCAP cycle and the formulation of the WBG’s next corporate strategy.

The United Nations Global Compact for Migration: 2023 Mid‑Term Review, UN Network on Migration Coordination, and Emerging Implementation Gaps

The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM) was adopted by consensus at the Intergovernmental Conference in Marrakech on 10 December 2018. As a non‑legally binding framework, it sets out 23 objectives covering the entire migration cycle. The United Nations Network on Migration (UNNM), established in 2018 and chaired by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), serves as the coordination mechanism for UN system‑wide support to GCM implementation.

The GCM’s review architecture comprises a quadrennial International Migration Review Forum (IMRF) and a mid‑term review conducted by the UNNM. The first IMRF took place in May 2022 in New York, producing a Progress Declaration that highlighted advances in data collection (Objective 1), migrant‑rights protection (Objective 7), and regular pathways (Objective 5). The UNNM’s mid‑term review, finalized in September 2023, synthesized voluntary national reports from 112 Member States, regional consultations, and thematic inputs from civil society and the private sector.

The 2023 mid‑term review identified three persistent implementation gaps. First, only 38 % of reporting countries have established a national coordination mechanism that brings together migration, labour, health, and foreign‑affairs ministries, leading to fragmented policy responses. Second, the “whole‑of‑government” approach to migrant‑vulnerability screening (Objective 8) remains under‑developed; fewer than 30 % of countries have standardized referral pathways for victims of trafficking, smuggling, or gender‑based violence. Third, financing for GCM‑aligned programmes is heavily reliant on earmarked Official Development Assistance (ODA); the review estimated that only 12 % of migration‑related ODA in 2022 was channelled through pooled or multi‑donor funds, limiting predictability and alignment with national priorities.

In response, the UNNM launched the “GCM Implementation Accelerator” in January 2024, a technical assistance facility funded by a US$15 million multi‑donor trust fund (contributions from the European Union, Germany, Canada, and the UN Migration Multi‑Partner Trust Fund). The Accelerator provides targeted support to 25 pilot countries for establishing national coordination mechanisms, developing migration‑sensitive labour market information systems, and designing blended‑finance projects that link diaspora investment with local development.

The review also emphasized the need for stronger linkages between the GCM and the 2030 Agenda. The 2023 SDG Summit’s Political Declaration explicitly referenced the GCM as a key vehicle for achieving SDG 10.7 (facilitate orderly, safe, regular migration). The UNNM’s 2024‑2025 workplan includes a joint mapping exercise with the UN Development System to align GCM indicators with SDG targets, and a “Global Migration Data Portal” upgrade to enable real‑time tracking of migration flows, remittance volumes, and policy changes.

Looking forward, the second IMRF is scheduled for 2026. The UNNM has proposed a “Voluntary GCM Commitment Platform” where Member States can announce concrete, time‑bound pledges — such as regularization campaigns, bilateral labour agreements, or climate‑migration adaptation plans — to be reviewed at the 2026 Forum. The platform aims to shift the GCM from a declaratory framework to an accountability‑driven agenda.

  • Confusing the AfCFTA Dispute Settlement Body’s cross‑retaliation rule with the WTO’s separate arbitration requirement; AfCFTA allows cross‑retaliation directly from the panel report.
  • Assuming the IMF Food Shock Window is a permanent facility; it is temporary and set to expire in April 2025 unless extended.
  • Believing the UN Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System scores are binding on troop‑contributing countries; they are diagnostic and trigger dialogue, not mandatory deployment.
  • Thinking the World Bank’s Climate Change Action Plan requires 50 % of all financing to be climate‑related; the 35 % target applies to climate co‑benefits, while the 50 % target refers to operations with a climate component.
  • Overlooking that the Global Compact for Migration’s mid‑term review is conducted by the UN Network on Migration, not by the International Migration Review Forum.
  • Assuming the AfCFTA Appellate Body is fully operational; as of 2024 it is not yet constituted and appeals are heard by ad‑hoc arbitration panels.
  • Confusing the IMF’s Food Shock Window eligibility with the Rapid Credit Facility’s general access; the FSW requires a specific food‑security policy statement and a demonstrated sharp deterioration in food‑security indicators.

The sections above provide the mechanistic detail, recent data points, and examiner‑focused nuances needed to answer advanced questions on these evolving governance instruments.

The International Atomic Energy Agency: Safeguards Verification, the Additional Protocol, and the Iran Nuclear Deal Architecture

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), established in 1957 under the Statute of the IAEA, operates as the global nuclear verification authority. Its safeguards system evolved from the 1968 Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) requirement under Article III for non-nuclear-weapon states to conclude Comprehensive Safeguards Agreements (CSAs) based on INFCIRC/153 (Corrected). The CSA grants the IAEA the right and obligation to verify the correctness and completeness of a state's declared nuclear material and activities. The verification toolkit includes nuclear material accountancy, containment and surveillance measures, and inspections — both routine and special. The 1997 Model Additional Protocol (INFCIRC/540) significantly expanded verification authority by granting the IAEA complementary access to undeclared sites, environmental sampling rights, and the requirement for states to provide expanded declarations covering the entire nuclear fuel cycle, from uranium mining to waste management. As of 2024, 139 states have Additional Protocols in force, while key NPT parties including Iran, Egypt, and Brazil have signed but not ratified, and Israel, India, and Pakistan remain outside the NPT framework entirely.

The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), concluded in Vienna on 14 July 2015 between Iran and the P5+1 (China, France, Germany, Russia, United Kingdom, United States) plus the European Union, created a unique verification architecture layered atop the CSA and Additional Protocol. Iran provisionally applied the Additional Protocol pending ratification, accepted enhanced monitoring under the "Roadmap for Clarification of Past and Present Outstanding Issues," and agreed to specific limits: enrichment capped at 3.67 % U-235, stockpile limited to 300 kg of UF6 equivalent, Fordow converted to a research centre with no enrichment, and the Arak reactor redesigned to minimize plutonium production. The JCPOA established the Joint Commission (meeting at ministerial and technical levels) and the Procurement Channel for dual-use goods, managed by the UN Security Council Resolution 2231 (2015) mechanism. The IAEA's verification burden expanded to include continuous online enrichment monitors, daily access to Natanz and Fordow, and managed access to military sites under a defined dispute resolution timeline (14 days for the Joint Commission, then 5 days for the Advisory Board, then 3 days for the Joint Commission again). The United States withdrew from the JCPOA on 8 May 2018 under Presidential Memorandum, reimposing secondary sanctions. Iran responded with calibrated breaches: exceeding stockpile limits (July 2019), enriching to 4.5 % (July 2019), 20 % (January 2021), and 60 % (April 2021), installing advanced centrifuge cascades (IR-2m, IR-4, IR-6), and restricting IAEA access by removing 27 surveillance cameras (June 2022). The IAEA Board of Governors adopted resolutions in June 2022 and November 2022 calling for cooperation on unexplained uranium traces at three undeclared sites (Varamin, Turquzabad, Marivan); Iran has not provided technically credible explanations as of the March 2024 Director General report. The JCPOA's "snapback" mechanism under UNSCR 2231 allows any JCPOA participant to trigger the reimposition of all UN sanctions within 30 days if the Security Council fails to adopt a resolution to continue sanctions relief — a mechanism the United States attempted to invoke in August 2020 but was rejected by the Security Council presidency on the grounds the US was no longer a participant.

The IAEA's safeguards budget for 2024 stands at €172.5 million, with 85 % funded by assessed contributions on the UN scale and 15 % by voluntary contributions (extrabudgetary). The Department of Safeguards employs approximately 1,000 staff, including 350 inspectors. The State-Level Concept (SLC), implemented since 2013, shifts from facility-by-facility verification to a holistic, state-level evaluation using acquisition path analysis and information-driven safeguards. The SLC requires the Annual Implementation Plan (AIP) for each state, integrating open-source intelligence, satellite imagery, export-controlled procurement data, and voluntary reporting. The IAEA's verification of the DPRK's nuclear programme remains limited to satellite imagery and open-source analysis since inspectors were expelled in April 2009; the 2023 Director General report noted continued operation of the 5 MWe reactor at Yongbyon, centrifuge enrichment at Kangson, and construction at the Punggye-ri nuclear test site. The IAEA also administers the Nuclear Security Series guidance, the Incident and Trafficking Database (ITDB) with 4,200+ confirmed incidents since 1993, and the Nuclear Safety Review following the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi accident, which led to the 2015 Vienna Declaration on Nuclear Safety and the 2017 Peer Review of the Convention on Nuclear Safety.

The International Maritime Organization: The 2023 GHG Strategy, Carbon Intensity Indicator, and the Mid-Term Measures Negotiation

The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a UN specialized agency since 1958, regulates international shipping through the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), and the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW). MARPOL Annex VI, adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005, addresses air pollution and energy efficiency. The 2011 amendments (Resolution MEPC.203(62)) made the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) for new ships and the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) for all ships mandatory from 1 January 2013 — the first legally binding global GHG reduction regime for an entire industry sector. The Initial IMO GHG Strategy, adopted at MEPC 72 in April 2018, set a vision to peak GHG emissions as soon as possible and reduce total annual GHG emissions by at least 50 % by 2050 compared to 2008, while pursuing efforts towards phasing them out. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted at MEPC 80 in July 2023, significantly raised ambition: a common aspiration for net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints of 20 % (striving for 30 %) reduction by 2030 and 70 % (striving for 80 %) by 2040, relative to 2008. The Strategy also commits to a basket of candidate mid-term measures combining a technical element (a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating the lifecycle GHG intensity of marine fuels) and an economic element (a GHG pricing mechanism), to be finalized by 2025 and enter into force by 2027.

The short-term measures already in force since 1 January 2023 (MEPC 76, June 2021) comprise the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) — a one-time certification requiring existing ships to meet a minimum energy efficiency level — and the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating scheme (Resolution MEPC.336(76)). The CII rates ships from A (best) to E (worst) based on the Attained Annual Operational CII (gCO2/dwt-nm) relative to a Required CII derived from a reference line tightened annually by 2 % (2023-2026), 3 % (2027-2030), and further thereafter. Ships rated D for three consecutive years or E for one year must submit a corrective action plan within their SEEMP. The CII applies to cargo ships, cruise ships, and LNG carriers of 5,000 GT and above — approximately 25,000 ships. The first reporting period (2023) data submitted by 31 March 2024 will establish the baseline; early analyses by classification societies suggest 15-20 % of the fleet may fall into D/E categories without operational changes (slow steaming, hull cleaning, propeller polishing, waste heat recovery). Developing countries, particularly small island developing states (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs), have raised concerns at MEPC 79 (December 2022) and MEPC 80 about disproportionate impacts on trade costs, food security, and the lack of an impact assessment methodology. The "Just Transition" concept was incorporated into the 2023 Strategy preamble, and a Capacity Building and Technical Cooperation framework is being developed under the IMO's Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme (ITCP).

The mid-term measures negotiation, launched at MEPC 80, follows a two-track workplan: the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) Intersessional Working Group on GHG (ISWG-GHG) meets three times per year. Candidate economic measures include: a flat levy on GHG emissions (proposed by the Marshall Islands, Solomon Islands, and the "Pacific Island States" group at $100-150/tonne CO2e), a feebate system (rebates for low-carbon fuels funded by levies on high-carbon fuels, proposed by Japan and Norway), a cap-and-trade emissions trading system (EU preference), and a reward-only mechanism (China, Brazil, Argentina, South Africa). The technical measure — the Global Fuel Standard (GFS) — will set maximum well-to-wake GHG intensity limits (gCO2e/MJ) for marine fuels, tightening over time, with compliance achieved through blending, alternative fuels (methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, biofuels), or purchasing compliance units. The lifecycle assessment (LCA) guidelines for marine fuels were finalized at MEPC 80 (Resolution MEPC.376(80)), defining default emission factors and certification pathways for sustainability (ILUC, land use, water). The 2024-2025 workplan targets: impact assessment completion by MEPC 82 (October 2024), legal text finalization by MEPC 83 (April 2025), and adoption by MEPC 84 (October 2025) for entry into force 16 months later under MARPOL Article 16 (tacit acceptance). The EU's inclusion of maritime transport in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) from January 2024 (40 % of verified emissions in 2024, 70 % in 2025, 100 % from 2026) and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation (GHG intensity targets from 2025) create parallel regulatory pressure; the IMO aims to avoid fragmentation through a globally harmonized regime. The United States, not a party to the Kyoto Protocol, participates actively in ISWG-GHG but opposes a universal levy, favouring a "goal-based" approach with national flexibility.

Examiner's Trap: Conflating IMO CII with EU ETS Maritime Scope
A question asks: "The Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) under MARPOL Annex VI and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) extension to maritime transport both apply to ships of 5,000 GT and above. Explain the operational difference in compliance obligation between the two regimes for a Panamax bulk carrier voyaging between Singapore and Rotterdam in 2024."
The CII is a flag-State certification and rating obligation applicable to the ship globally regardless of voyage. The ship must calculate its Attained Annual Operational CII for the entire calendar year 2023 (reported by 31 March 2024) across all voyages, and if rated D/E, submit a corrective action plan to its flag Administration or Recognized Organization. The EU ETS maritime obligation is a voyage-based surrender obligation for the shipping company (defined as the ISM Company). For the Singapore-Rotterdam voyage, only 50 % of the voyage emissions (departure from non-EU port to arrival at EU port) fall under EU ETS in 2024 (40 % surrender rate). The company must purchase and surrender EU Allowances (EUAs) for that portion by 30 September 2025. CII non-compliance risks detention/port State control; EU ETS non-compliance risks financial penalties (€100/tonne CO2 excess) and expulsion order after two consecutive years. They operate in parallel; compliance with one does not satisfy the other.
Exam-Day Strategy: IMO GHG Regime Layering
Memorize the three-layer timeline: (1) EEDI/SEEMP (2013) — design/management baseline; (2) EEXI/CII (2023) — operational efficiency rating for existing fleet; (3) Mid-term measures (2027 target) — Global Fuel Standard + GHG pricing. For each layer, know the legal instrument (MARPOL Annex VI regulation number), the metric (gCO2/tonne-nm vs gCO2e/MJ), and the compliance entity (ship vs company). The 2023 Strategy checkpoints (2030/2040/2050) are indicative, not legally binding — only the mid-term measures will create binding targets. Distinguish "well-to-wake" (Lifecycle, LCA) from "tank-to-wake" (combustion only) — the GFS uses well-to-wake.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations: Centrality, the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific, and the Dispute Settlement Mechanism Under the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), established by the Bangkok Declaration of 8 August 1967, comprises ten Member States: Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar, and Cambodia. The ASEAN Charter, which entered into force on 15 December 2008, conferred legal personality, established the ASEAN Summit (biannual), the ASEAN Coordinating Council, the three Community Councils (Political-Security, Economic, Socio-Cultural), the ASEAN Secretariat in Jakarta, and the Committee of Permanent Representatives (CPR). Decision-making remains consensus-based ("ASEAN Way"), with the ASEAN Minus X formula allowing flexible participation for economic integration initiatives. The ASEAN Community Vision 2025, adopted at the 27th Summit in Kuala Lumpur (November 2015), succeeds the 2015 Community blueprints across three pillars: the ASEAN Political-Security Community (APSC), the ASEAN Economic Community (AEC), and the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community (ASCC). The AEC 2025 Consolidated Strategic Action Plan targets a highly integrated economy: the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement (ATIGA) has eliminated tariffs on 98.6 % of tariff lines for ASEAN-6 and 91.4 % for CLMV (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam); the ASEAN Comprehensive Investment Agreement (ACIA) provides investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS); and the ASEAN Framework Agreement on Services (AFAS) has completed ten packages of commitments. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), signed 15 November 2020 and entered into force 1 January 2022, anchors ASEAN centrality in the regional trade architecture by linking ASEAN with its five FTA partners (China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand) under a single rules-of-origin regime.

The ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP), adopted at the 34th Summit in Bangkok (June 2019), articulates ASEAN's collective response to competing Indo-Pacific narratives (US "Free and Open Indo-Pacific", Japan's FOIP, India's Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative, China's Global Security Initiative). The AOIP rests on four principles: (1) openness, transparency, inclusivity, rules-based order; (2) respect for sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity; (3) peaceful dispute settlement per UN Charter and UNCLOS; (4) ASEAN centrality as the underlying architecture. It identifies four cooperation areas: maritime cooperation, connectivity, SDGs 2030, and economic cooperation. The AOIP explicitly rejects bloc-based confrontation and calls for existing ASEAN-led mechanisms — the East Asia Summit (EAS), the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF), the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) — to serve as the primary platforms for Indo-Pacific dialogue. The 2023 ASEAN Leaders' Declaration on the AOIP Implementation (Jakarta, September 2023) established the AOIP Plan of Action (2023-2027) with 82 concrete activities, including a maritime domain awareness network, a cybersecurity capacity-building programme, and a sustainable infrastructure standard aligned with the ASEAN Connectivity Master Plan 2025.

The Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC), signed in 1976 and amended in 1987 (Protocol) and 1998 (accession by non-ASEAN states), is ASEAN's foundational political instrument. As of 2024, 54 High Contracting Parties include all ten ASEAN members, all ten ASEAN Dialogue Partners, and major powers (US, China, Russia, India, EU, UK, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand). The TAC establishes the High Council — a dispute settlement mechanism comprising a Ministerial Council and a Conciliation Commission — for disputes between High Contracting Parties that cannot be resolved by peaceful means of their own choice (Article 14). The High Council has never been convened since 1976. The South China Sea disputes illustrate the limitation: claimant states (Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei) and non-claimant ASEAN members have not invoked the TAC High Council against China (a High Contracting Party since 2003). Instead, the Philippines initiated arbitration under UNCLOS Annex VII in 2013 (PCA Case No. 2013-19), resulting in the 12 July 2016 Award. ASEAN's collective response has been the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC, 2002) and the ongoing negotiation of a Code of Conduct (COC). The COC negotiations, guided by the 2018 Single Draft Negotiating Text (SDNT) and the 2021 Provisional Agreement on the Preamble and Section 1, face deadlock over: (a) geographic scope (whether to include the Taiwan Strait, Natuna Sea), (b) legal bindingness (China prefers "politically binding"), (c) dispute settlement mechanism (China opposes third-party compulsory procedures), and (d) the status of the 2016 Arbitral Award. The 2023 ASEAN-China Joint Statement on the 20th Anniversary of the DOC reaffirmed commitment to complete the COC within the "early conclusion" timeline (target 2026), but the 52nd ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting (Jakarta, July 2023) acknowledged "challenges" without specifying breakthroughs.

The United Nations Regular Budget and Scale of Assessments: Methodology, the 2022-2024 Scale, and Article 19 Arrears

The United Nations regular budget, approved by the General Assembly under Article 17 of the Charter, funds the Secretariat, the International Court of Justice, special political missions, and the UN's share of jointly financed organs (e.g., UNOG, UNOV). The budget period shifted from biennial to annual in 2020 (Resolution 73/273) to improve agility; the 2024 budget stands at $3.59 billion (net of staff assessment). The Scale of Assessments, the methodology for apportioning expenses among Member States, is determined by the Committee on Contributions (18 members elected by the General Assembly for three-year terms) and approved by the Assembly every three years. The methodology, established in 1946 and refined through successive resolutions (latest: Resolution 76/238 for the 2022-2024 scale), uses a capacity-to-pay principle based on Gross National Income (GNI) averages over a base period (2016-2018 for the 2022-2024 scale), adjusted for: (a) a floor of 0.001 % (minimum assessment), (b) a ceiling of 22 % (maximum for any single Member — currently the United States), (c) a least developed country (LDC) ceiling of 0.01 %, (d) a debt-burden adjustment for heavily indebted poor countries, and (e) a per capita income adjustment (the "gradient") that reduces the share of low-income countries and increases that of high-income countries relative to raw GNI shares. The 2022-2024 scale (Resolution 76/238, adopted 24 December 2021) sets the top ten contributors as: USA (22.000 %), China (15.254 %), Japan (8.033 %), Germany (6.111 %), UK (4.375 %), France (4.318 %), Italy (3.189 %), Canada (2.628 %), South Korea (2.574 %), Russia (2.405 %). India's assessment rose from 0.834 % (2019-2021) to 1.044 % (2022-2024), reflecting GNI growth. The scale also determines assessments for peacekeeping operations (separate scale with discounts for developing countries) and international tribunals.

Article 19 of the Charter provides that a Member State in arrears equal to or exceeding the contributions due for the preceding two full years loses its vote in the General Assembly, unless the Assembly is satisfied that the failure to pay is due to conditions beyond the Member's control. As of 31 December 2023, seven Member States were subject to Article 19: Comoros, Ecuador, Lebanon, Libya, Somalia, South Sudan, and Venezuela. The General Assembly has routinely adopted resolutions (e.g., Resolution 78/248, December 2023) granting vote-retention exemptions for Comoros, Somalia, and South Sudan on grounds of conflict and institutional collapse; for Libya, exemptions have been granted annually since 2014. Venezuela and Lebanon have not received exemptions since 2021 and 2022 respectively, and thus lost voting rights. The United States, while not in technical arrears under the two-year rule due to its practice of paying assessed contributions late in the calendar year (often December), accumulates significant "current-year" arrears; as of September 2023, the US owed $686 million to the regular budget (19 % of assessed contributions for 2023). The Capital Master Plan (CMP), the renovation of UN Headquarters (2008-2021), was financed through a separate assessment scale (the "CMP scale") with a total cost of $2.15 billion; the final assessment was issued in 2022. The UN's cash-flow crisis — driven by late payments from major contributors — has repeatedly forced the Secretary-General to impose hiring freezes, defer maintenance, and prioritize mandated activities; the 2023 "Cash Management Strategy" (A/78/347) introduced a liquidity reserve target of $150 million and monthly cash forecasting.

The Committee on Contributions' 2024 session (June 2024) will initiate the review for the 2025-2027 scale, using the 2019-2021 GNI base period. Key methodological debates include: (1) the use of Market Exchange Rates (MER) vs Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) — the current methodology uses MER (Atlas method), which inflates the shares of countries with strong currencies and undervalues large developing economies; India and Brazil have advocated for PPP-based GNI. (2) The gradient formula — the current piecewise linear gradient (Resolution 55/5 B) has not been recalibrated since 2000; high-income countries argue it over-corrects, while middle-income countries argue it under-corrects. (3) The ceiling — the US has pressed for a reduction from 22 % to 20 % (matching the peacekeeping ceiling), while the G77 opposes any change without addressing the floor and LDC ceiling simultaneously. (4) Arrears management — proposals for a "multi-year payment plan" framework for Article 19 cases, and a "timely payment incentive" (discount for early payment), have been discussed in the Fifth Committee but not adopted. The 2024 Scale Review will also consider the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on 2020-2021 GNI data, with some members requesting a "pandemic adjustment" clause.

The International Law Commission: Draft Articles on State Responsibility, Prevention of Transboundary Harm, and the Protection of the Atmosphere

The International Law Commission (ILC), established by the General Assembly in 1947 (Resolution 174 (II)) under Article 13(1)(a) of the Charter, comprises 34 members elected for five-year terms as individuals of recognized competence in international law. Its mandate is the progressive development and codification of international law. The ILC's output takes the form of Draft Articles with commentaries, submitted to the General Assembly for action — typically adoption as a convention, a declaration, or referral to a diplomatic conference. Three completed projects form the backbone of modern state responsibility and environmental liability regimes. The Draft Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA), adopted on first reading in 2001 (Resolution 56/83) and commended to governments on second reading, codify the secondary rules of state responsibility. Key provisions: Article 2 defines an internationally wrongful act as conduct attributable to the state under international law that constitutes a breach of an international obligation. Articles 4-11 detail attribution: conduct of state organs (Article 4), persons exercising governmental authority (Article 5), organs placed at disposal of another state (Article 6), ultra vires conduct (Article 7), conduct directed/controlled by a state (Article 8), conduct in absence of official authorities (Article 9), and conduct of insurrectional movements (Article 10). Article 12 defines breach; Articles 13-14 distinguish continuing and composite breaches. Articles 15-16 address circumstances precluding wrongfulness: consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure, distress, necessity. Articles 28-41 establish the content of responsibility: cessation, non-repetition, full reparation (restitution, compensation, satisfaction). Articles 42-48 regulate the invocation of responsibility by injured states and states other than injured states (Article 48 — obligations erga omnes and erga omnes partes). Articles 49-54 govern countermeasures: they must be proportionate, reversible, and preceded by a demand for compliance (Article 52). The ICJ has repeatedly affirmed ARSIWA as reflective of customary international law (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997, Arrest Warrant 2002, Bosnia v. Serbia 2007, Jadhav 2019).

The Draft Articles on Prevention of Transboundary Harm from Hazardous Activities, adopted in 2001 (Resolution 56/82), address the primary obligation of prevention for activities not prohibited by international law but involving a risk of significant transboundary harm. Article 3 establishes the obligation to take all appropriate measures to prevent significant transboundary harm or minimize the risk. Articles 7-14 elaborate the due diligence standard: risk assessment (Article 7), notification and consultation (Articles 8-10), emergency preparedness (Article 11), and cooperation (Articles 12-14). The commentary clarifies that "significant" harm excludes de minimis impacts, and "hazardous activities" are those creating a risk of significant harm (e.g., nuclear installations, chemical plants, large dams, genetically modified organisms). The ILC deliberately avoided a strict liability regime, leaving liability to a separate future instrument. The 2006 Draft Principles on the Allocation of Loss in the Case of Transboundary Harm Arising out of Hazardous Activities (Resolution 61/36) complement the prevention articles by addressing civil liability: Principle 4 requires the state of origin to ensure prompt and adequate compensation; Principle 9 encourages strict liability regimes; Principle 12 addresses shared liability for multiple sources. These instruments informed the 2010 Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol on Liability and Redress to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, and the 1997 UN Watercourses Convention (Article 12 on notification).

The Draft Articles on Protection of the Atmosphere, adopted on second reading in 2021 (Resolution 76/117) and commended to the General Assembly, represent the ILC's most recent major codification. The 22 Draft Articles address the obligation to protect the atmosphere (Article 3), the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) (Article 4), the obligation not to cause significant transboundary atmospheric harm (Article 5), and the duty to cooperate (Article 6). Article 7 establishes the framework approach: states shall adopt legislative, administrative, and other measures. Articles 8-10 cover monitoring, assessment, and information exchange. Articles 11-13 address atmospheric degradation from specific sources: stratospheric ozone depletion (cross-referencing the Vienna Convention/Montreal Protocol), climate change (cross-referencing UNFCCC/Paris Agreement), and transboundary air pollution (cross-referencing the 1979 CLRTAP). Article 14 addresses activities in areas beyond national jurisdiction. Articles 15-17 cover scientific and technical cooperation, capacity building, and technology transfer. Articles 18-20 address dispute settlement, relationship with other obligations, and the protection of the atmosphere in armed conflict. The Draft Articles are deliberately non-duplicative of existing treaty regimes; they provide an overarching customary law framework that fills gaps (e.g., black carbon, short-lived climate pollutants, solar radiation modification governance) and reinforces the procedural obligations (notification, consultation, EIA) that apply across atmospheric threats. The General Assembly has not yet convened a diplomatic conference; the Draft Articles remain a "commendation" text, but the ICJ's 2024 Advisory Opinion on Climate Change Obligations (requested by UNGA Resolution 77/276) is expected to reference the ILC's work on due diligence, CBDR-RC, and the no-harm principle as evidence of customary law.

  • Confusing the IAEA Additional Protocol's "complementary access" with the "special inspection" under the CSA; complementary access is broader, applies to undeclared sites, and does not require the same 24-hour notice period as special inspections.
  • Assuming the IMO CII rating (A-E) is a certification requirement like the International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate (IAPP); the CII is an operational rating reported annually, while the IAPP certifies statutory equipment and EEDI/EEXI compliance.
  • Believing the ASEAN High Council under the TAC has been used for the South China Sea disputes; it has never been convened since 1976 — the Philippines chose UNCLOS Annex VII arbitration instead.
  • Thinking the UN Scale of Assessments uses Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) GNI; it uses Market Exchange Rate (Atlas method) GNI, which significantly affects the assessed shares of large developing economies.
  • Conflating the ILC Draft Articles on State Responsibility (ARSIWA) with the Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection; ARSIWA governs state-to-state responsibility, while Diplomatic Protection governs the state's right to espouse claims of its nationals.
  • Assuming the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy's 2030/2040 checkpoints are legally binding targets; they are "indicative checkpoints" — only the mid-term measures (GFS + pricing) to be adopted by 2025 will create binding obligations.
  • Overlooking that the IAEA's State-Level Concept (SLC) replaced the criteria-based approach for all states with CSAs in force, not just those with Additional Protocols; the SLC uses acquisition path analysis even for states without APs, though AP information enhances the evaluation.

The International Court of Justice’s Contentious Jurisdiction: Optional Clause Declarations, Reservations, and Recent Case Law

The ICJ’s contentious jurisdiction rests on the consent of states, expressed principally through the Optional Clause of Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute. As of December 2023, 73 states have deposited declarations accepting the Court’s compulsory jurisdiction. The declarations vary widely: some are unconditional (e.g., Norway, Sweden), while most contain reservations that limit the scope of acceptance. The United States’ 1946 declaration, for example, excludes disputes “essentially within the domestic jurisdiction” of the United States, a reservation the Court upheld in Nicaragua v. United States (1986). China’s 2006 declaration excludes disputes concerning “sovereignty, territorial integrity, or maritime delimitation” — a reservation that effectively removes the South China Sea disputes from compulsory jurisdiction.

Reservations are subject to the Court’s scrutiny under the “reciprocity” principle: a state may invoke another’s reservation only to the extent that it has accepted the same limitation. In Armed Activities on the Territory of the Congo (DRC v. Uganda, 2005), the Court held that Uganda could not rely on its own reservation to avoid jurisdiction because the DRC’s declaration did not contain a matching reservation. The Court also applies the “vital interest” test: a reservation that defeats the object and purpose of the Optional Clause may be deemed invalid, though the Court has rarely struck down reservations outright.

Recent case law illustrates how the Court navigates these declarations. In Nicaragua v. Colombia (Judgment of 13 July 2023), the Court exercised jurisdiction based on Colombia’s 1999 declaration accepting compulsory jurisdiction “in respect of all legal disputes” and Nicaragua’s 1929 declaration (as successor to the 1928 declaration). Colombia’s reservation excluding “disputes concerning the interpretation or application of treaties concluded before 1948” did not cover the 1928 Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation, allowing the Court to rule on maritime delimitation. In Ukraine v. Russian Federation (Order of 16 March 2022 on provisional measures), the Court found prima facie jurisdiction under the Genocide Convention’s Article IX, which contains its own compromissory clause, independent of Optional Clause declarations. The Court ordered Russia to suspend military operations, a measure Russia has not complied with, highlighting the enforcement gap.

The 2023 Gambia v. Myanmar case (Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide) proceeded on the basis of the Genocide Convention’s Article IX, again bypassing Optional Clause reservations. The Court’s 2023 provisional measures order required Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts against the Rohingya. These cases demonstrate that while Optional Clause declarations remain a cornerstone of the Court’s docket, compromissory clauses in multilateral treaties increasingly provide alternative jurisdictional bases, reducing the practical impact of reservations.

The IMF Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust: Design, Eligibility, and the 2022‑2023 Reforms

The Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT) is the IMF’s concessional financing window for low‑income countries (LICs). Established in 1987 as the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility and renamed in 1999, the PRGT provides zero‑interest loans with a 10‑year grace period and 20‑year maturity. Eligibility is tied to the International Development Association (IDA) per‑capita income threshold, which for FY 2024 stands at US $1,135. Countries above the threshold but deemed “blend” (eligible for both PRGT and non‑concessional resources) may access the PRGT under the “blend” terms, which carry a modest interest rate (0.5 % per annum).

The PRGT operates through three main facilities: the Extended Credit Facility (ECF) for medium‑term balance‑of‑payments support, the Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) for urgent needs with limited conditionality, and the Standby Credit Facility (SCF) for precautionary purposes. Access limits are expressed as a percentage of quota: the ECF norm is 145 % of quota (cumulative 435 %), the RCF 100 % (cumulative 150 %), and the SCF 145 % (cumulative 435 %). The 2022 PRGT Review, concluded in June 2022, raised the annual access limit for the ECF to 180 % of quota and the cumulative limit to 540 % for countries facing exceptional shocks, reflecting the pandemic’s fiscal impact.

A major 2023 reform introduced the “Climate Resilience Window” (CRW) within the PRGT, financed by a dedicated trust fund capitalised through bilateral contributions and SDR rechanneling. The CRW provides additional concessional financing (up to 50 % of quota) for climate‑adaptation projects that meet the IMF’s “macro‑critical” criteria. The first CRW‑supported arrangement was approved for Rwanda in October 2023, linking disbursements to measurable climate‑resilience indicators. The reform also streamlined conditionality: the 2022 Conditionality Review mandated that PRGT programs prioritize “country‑owned” structural reforms, reduce prior actions, and incorporate social‑spending floors calibrated to the Sustainable Development Goals.

Governance of the PRGT rests with the IMF’s Executive Board, but the Trust’s resources are legally separate from the General Resources Account. The 2023 replenishment round (PRGT‑2023) secured SDR 12.5 billion in new loan resources and SDR 2.5 billion in subsidy resources, bringing total PRGT lending capacity to SDR 38 billion. The replenishment introduced a “graduation” mechanism: countries that exceed the IDA threshold for two consecutive years begin a phased transition to non‑concessional financing, with a three‑year grace period during which they may still access the PRGT at blend terms.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the IMF’s Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT) is correct? (a) PRGT loans carry a market‑based interest rate. (b) The PRGT is financed entirely from the IMF’s General Resources Account. (c) The 2022 PRGT Review raised the annual ECF access limit to 180 % of quota. (d) Only countries below the IDA income threshold can ever access the PRGT.”
Correct answer: (c). PRGT loans are concessional (zero interest for the poorest, 0.5 % for blend). The PRGT’s resources are legally separate from the General Resources Account, financed by bilateral loan contributions and subsidy resources. The 2022 Review indeed raised the annual ECF access limit to 180 % of quota and the cumulative limit to 540 % for exceptional cases. Blend countries above the IDA threshold may still access the PRGT under blend terms, so (d) is false.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three PRGT facilities (ECF, RCF, SCF) and their standard access limits (145 %/100 %/145 % of quota). Note the 2022 Review’s upward revision to 180 %/540 % for ECF. Remember the Climate Resilience Window launched in 2023 and the graduation rule for blend countries. A quick table in your notes linking facility, purpose, interest rate, and access limit will save time on multiple‑choice and short‑answer questions.

UN Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System: Force Generation, Performance Metrics, and the 2023 Reforms

The Capability Readiness System (PCRS) was launched in 2015 to replace the ad‑hoc “force generation” model with a predictable, tiered pipeline of military and police contributions. Member states register pledged units — infantry battalions, engineering companies, medical units, formed police units — into three readiness levels: Level 1 (ready to deploy within 30 days), Level 2 (ready within 90 days), and Level 3 (developing capability, 180 days). As of the 2023 Peacekeeping Ministerial in Accra, 112 countries had registered 1,842 pledged units, of which 62 % were at Level 1 or Level 2.

Performance metrics were introduced in 2021 through the “Performance‑Based Incentive Mechanism” (PBIM). Units are evaluated on four pillars: operational readiness (equipment serviceability, training certification), conduct and discipline (zero‑tolerance compliance, SEA prevention), gender parity (minimum 15 % women in formed units by 2025), and sustainability (environmental footprint, medical self‑sufficiency). Scores feed into a “readiness index” that determines priority for deployment and eligibility for the UN’s “Premium Reimbursement Rate” — a 10 % uplift on the standard troop‑cost reimbursement for Level 1 units meeting all pillars.

The 2023 reforms, endorsed by the Security Council in Resolution 2695 (2023), added two structural changes. First, a “Pledging Conference Cycle” was institutionalised: biennial high‑level meetings where troop‑contributing countries (TCCs) announce new pledges and upgrade existing ones, replacing the previous ad‑hoc requests. Second, the “Rapid Deployment Enabler” (RDE) was created — a standing pool of pre‑positioned strategic airlift and engineering assets funded by assessed contributions, reducing the average deployment lead time from 90 to 45 days for Level 1 units. The RDE’s first activation was the rapid insertion of a Bangladeshi engineering company into MONUSCO in March 2024.

Despite these advances, gaps persist. The 2023 Secretary‑General’s report (A/78/321) noted that only 38 % of pledged Level 1 units met the gender‑parity target, and 27 % of Level 2 units lacked certified medical self‑sufficiency. The report also highlighted the “capability‑commitment mismatch”: several major TCCs pledge high‑capability units but maintain them at Level 3 due to domestic operational tempo. The PCRS now includes a “commitment‑verification” audit, conducted by the Department of Peace Operations’ Force Generation Service, to flag such discrepancies before the pledging conference.

The International Labour Organization’s Maritime Labour Convention 2006: Entry into Force, 2022 Amendments, and Flag‑State Compliance

The Maritime Labour Convention (MLC), 2006 — often called the “seafarers’ bill of rights” — entered into force on 20 August 2013, twelve months after the 30th ratification by a member state representing at least 33 % of world gross tonnage. As of December 2023, 101 ILO member states have ratified, covering approximately 91 % of global gross tonnage. The Convention consolidates 68 existing maritime labour instruments into a single framework setting minimum standards for seafarers’ working conditions, accommodation, health protection, and social security.

The MLC’s unique “no‑more‑favourable‑treatment” clause (Article VII) requires that any national law providing better protection than the Convention prevails, preventing a race to the bottom. Compliance is monitored through a dual system: flag‑state inspections (certification of ships) and port‑state control (PSC) under regional memoranda of understanding such as the Paris MoU and Tokyo MoU. Ships of 500 GT and above engaged in international voyages must carry a Maritime Labour Certificate (MLC) and a Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance (DMLC) Parts I and II.

In June 2022, the International Labour Conference adopted a package of amendments (Resolution I/2022) that entered into force on 23 December 2023. Key changes include: (1) mandatory repatriation of seafarers abandoned due to pandemic‑related restrictions, with flag states required to maintain a financial security system; (2) expanded occupational health provisions covering mental‑health support and telemedicine; (3) new social‑security standards aligning with the ILO’s Social Security (Minimum Standards) Convention, 1952 (No. 102), requiring flag states to ensure coverage for sickness, unemployment, and old‑age benefits; (4) strengthened PSC guidelines allowing detention for “serious deficiencies” in MLC compliance, including lack of valid financial security for repatriation.

Flag‑state compliance remains uneven. The ILO’s Committee of Experts on the Application of Conventions and Recommendations (CEACR) noted in its 2023 report that 18 ratifying states had not yet enacted the 2022 amendments into national law, and 7 states had not submitted the required biennial reports. The Paris MoU’s 2023 annual report recorded 1,214 MLC‑related deficiencies, with 87 detentions — a 12 % increase over 2022 — primarily for missing DMLC Part II and inadequate financial security. The ILO has launched a “Flag State Capacity‑Building Programme” (2023‑2026) targeting the 18 non‑compliant states, funded through voluntary contributions from the International Transport Workers’ Federation and the International Chamber of Shipping.

The UN Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration: Objectives, Implementation Review, and the 2022 International Migration Review Forum

The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM) was adopted by consensus at the Intergovernmental Conference in Marrakech on 10‑11 December 2018 and endorsed by the UN General Assembly in Resolution 73/195 (2019). The Compact is a non‑legally binding cooperative framework comprising 23 objectives grouped under four guiding principles: people‑centred, international cooperation, national sovereignty, and sustainable development. Objectives range from collecting accurate migration data (Objective 1) to ensuring access to basic services for migrants (Objective 15) and facilitating safe, orderly return and readmission (Objective 21).

Implementation is reviewed through the International Migration Review Forum (IMRF), convened every four years under the auspices of the General Assembly. The first IMRF took place in New York on 17‑20 May 2022, attended by 152 member states, 300 civil‑society organisations, and UN agencies. The Forum’s outcome document (A/RES/76/266) highlighted progress on data harmonisation (the UN‑DESA “Migration Data Portal” launched in 2021), the expansion of regular pathways (e.g., Canada’s “Global Skills Strategy” and Germany’s “Skilled Immigration Act”), and the integration of migration into national development plans (e.g., Kenya’s “National Migration Policy” 2022).

However, the 2022 Forum identified persistent gaps: (1) insufficient protection for migrant children — only 38 % of states reported dedicated child‑protection mechanisms; (2) limited progress on climate‑induced displacement — the Compact’s Objective 2 (minimising adverse drivers) lacks a dedicated financing mechanism; (3) uneven implementation of the “whole‑of‑government” approach — 62 % of states reported inter‑ministerial coordination bodies, but only 27 % had allocated dedicated budgets. The Forum called for a “GCM Trust Fund” to support capacity‑building in developing countries, a proposal still under negotiation in the Fifth Committee.

The next IMRF is scheduled for 2026. In preparation, the UN Network on Migration (established 2018) has issued a “GCM Implementation Guide” (2023) with indicators for each objective, and the Secretary‑General’s 2024 report (A/79/210) will assess the Compact’s contribution to the 2030 Agenda. The GCM’s non‑binding nature means its impact depends on political will; the 2022 Forum demonstrated that peer‑review and voluntary reporting can generate momentum, but the absence of enforcement mechanisms remains a structural limitation.

  • Confusing the ICJ’s Optional Clause declarations with compromissory clauses in treaties; the former are unilateral, the latter are treaty‑based and often broader.
  • Assuming PRGT loans are interest‑free for all recipients; blend‑country borrowers pay 0.5 % and face different access limits.
  • Believing the PCRS automatically guarantees deployment; pledged units must pass the Performance‑Based Incentive Mechanism and readiness audits.
  • Thinking the MLC 2006 applies to all ships regardless of size; it covers ships of 500 GT and above on international voyages, with limited application to smaller vessels.
  • Treating the Global Compact for Migration as a legally binding treaty; it is a non‑binding political declaration with a voluntary review mechanism.
  • Overlooking that the 2022 MLC amendments entered into force only in December 2023; flag states had a 12‑month transition period.
  • Assuming the IMF’s Climate Resilience Window is a separate facility; it is an additional financing window within the PRGT, not a standalone trust.

UN Peacebuilding Fund Allocation Mechanisms and Results‑Based Financing

The UN Peacebuilding Fund (PBF) was established by the Secretary‑General in 2005 and formally endorsed by the General Assembly in resolution 60/180. It operates through three financing windows: the Immediate Response Facility (IRF) for rapid disbursement within 30 days of a crisis, the Peacebuilding and Recovery Facility (PRF) for medium‑term programmes, and a Results‑Based Financing (RBF) pilot launched in 2022 following the 2020 Peacebuilding Architecture Review. The PBF is governed by the Peacebuilding Support Office (PBSO) under the oversight of an Advisory Group composed of member‑state representatives, UN entities, and civil‑society organisations. Allocation decisions are guided by a conflict‑risk index, national ownership indicators, and a results framework that links each tranche to verifiable milestones such as the adoption of a transitional justice law or the demobilisation of a defined number of combatants.

In 2022 the PBF disbursed approximately US$300 million across 30 countries, with the largest shares going to the Central African Republic, Somalia, and Afghanistan. The RBF pilot introduced a performance‑based allocation model: 60 % of the approved envelope is released upfront, while the remaining 40 % is contingent on independent verification of pre‑agreed output indicators by the PBSO’s Monitoring and Evaluation Unit. The 2023 PBF Annual Report noted that 78 % of RBF‑linked milestones were met on schedule, prompting the Advisory Group to recommend scaling the model to all PRF allocations from 2024. A key operational challenge remains the timeliness of national reporting; the PBSO has therefore instituted a quarterly “Results Dashboard” that feeds directly into the Fund’s allocation algorithm.

Financing for the PBF is entirely voluntary. The 2023 pledging conference secured commitments of US$1.1 billion for the 2024‑2026 cycle, a 12 % increase over the previous cycle. The top contributors — Germany, the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Canada — together accounted for 55 % of pledged amounts. The Fund’s governance also includes a “Gender‑Responsive Allocation” marker, introduced in 2021, which requires that at least 15 % of each country‑level programme budget be earmarked for activities that directly address women’s participation in peace processes. Compliance with this marker is tracked through the PBSO’s annual gender audit, the results of which are reported to the Peacebuilding Commission’s annual session.

World Bank Climate Change Action Plan 2021‑2025: Mainstreaming Climate Finance in IDA and IBRD Operations

The World Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) 2021‑2025, approved by the Board of Executive Directors in June 2021, sets a target of directing 35 % of total financing to climate‑related activities by FY2025. The plan operationalises this target through three pillars: (1) mainstreaming climate screening into every Country Partnership Framework (CPF) and project appraisal; (2) expanding the use of the Climate Co‑Benefits methodology to quantify mitigation and adaptation outcomes; and (3) scaling up dedicated climate finance instruments such as the Climate Investment Funds (CIF) and the newly created Climate Finance Facility (CFF) under the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD).

Under the first pillar, the Bank introduced the Climate Change Screening Tool (CCST) in 2022, which assigns a climate risk rating (low, moderate, high) to each proposed operation. Projects rated high must incorporate a Climate Resilience Addendum and allocate at least 10 % of their budget to adaptation measures. The second pillar relies on the Climate Co‑Benefits methodology, updated in 2023, which applies a standardised coefficient to each sector — energy, transport, agriculture, water — to estimate tonnes of CO₂ equivalent avoided or sequestered. The 2023 World Bank Climate Finance Report showed that climate‑tagged commitments reached US$31.7 billion in FY2023, representing 31 % of total commitments, up from 26 % in FY2022.

The International Development Association (IDA) 20th replenishment (IDA20), concluded in December 2021, earmarked US$93 billion for the 2022‑2025 cycle, with a dedicated “Climate Window” of US$12 billion. The IBRD’s 2023 capital increase of US$13 billion further expanded the Bank’s capacity to issue green bonds, which financed US$8.4 billion of climate projects in FY2023. The CCAP also mandates that all new CPFs include a “Climate Change Diagnostic” chapter, a requirement that has been incorporated into 92 % of CPFs approved since 2022. The 2023 mid‑term review of the CCAP highlighted two implementation gaps: (i) insufficient granularity in adaptation metrics at the sub‑national level, and (ii) limited private‑sector mobilisation through the CFF, which leveraged only US$1.2 billion of private capital against a target of US$5 billion by 2025.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the World Bank’s Climate Co‑Benefits methodology translates sectoral investments into quantified climate outcomes, and identify one limitation noted in the 2023 mid‑term review.”
The Climate Co‑Benefits methodology applies sector‑specific coefficients — for example, 0.45 tCO₂e per US$1 million invested in renewable energy, 0.30 tCO₂e per US$1 million in sustainable transport — to convert financial commitments into estimated mitigation or adaptation results. These coefficients are derived from the Bank’s portfolio‑level historical data and are updated annually. The 2023 mid‑term review flagged that the methodology lacks granularity for adaptation outcomes at the sub‑national level, making it difficult to verify resilience benefits for vulnerable communities.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question references a specific Bank instrument (CCST, CFF, IDA Climate Window), cite the year of introduction and the quantitative target (e.g., 35 % climate finance by FY2025). Pair the instrument with its governance layer — Board approval, CPF integration, or private‑capital leverage — to demonstrate institutional depth.

UN Convention on the Law of the Sea: The 2023 ITLOS Advisory Opinion on State Obligations Regarding Climate Change

In December 2022 the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law (COSIS) submitted a request to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) for an advisory opinion on the obligations of States Parties to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) concerning marine pollution from anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The Tribunal delivered its opinion on 23 May 2023, constituting the first authoritative judicial pronouncement linking UNCLOS to climate change.

The opinion, adopted by a 21‑to‑0 majority, held that Article 194(1) of UNCLOS — which obliges States to “take all measures necessary to prevent, reduce and control pollution of the marine environment” — applies to GHG emissions that reach the oceans. The Tribunal clarified that the due‑diligence standard under Article 194 requires States to adopt domestic legislation, set emission‑reduction targets consistent with the best available science, and cooperate through relevant international organisations, notably the UNFCCC. It further stated that the principle of “common but differentiated responsibilities” (CBDR) informs the content of the due‑diligence obligation but does not relieve any State of the duty to act.

While advisory opinions are not legally binding, they carry significant interpretive weight. The ITLOS opinion has already been cited in the 2023 UNFCCC Global Stocktake technical dialogue and in the International Court of Justice’s 2024 advisory proceedings on climate obligations. Notably, the Tribunal refrained from prescribing specific emission‑reduction pathways, leaving the determination of “necessary measures” to each State’s sovereign discretion, subject to the due‑diligence benchmark. The opinion also addressed the relationship between UNCLOS and the Paris Agreement, affirming that the two regimes are complementary and that compliance with the Paris Agreement constitutes a strong, though not exclusive, indication of meeting UNCLOS obligations.

Quad Vaccine Partnership: COVAX Coordination, Manufacturing Hubs, and the 2023 Delhi Summit Outcomes

The Quad Vaccine Partnership (QVP) was announced at the first Quad Leaders’ Summit in March 2021, with the goal of delivering at least one billion COVID‑19 vaccine doses to the Indo‑Pacific and beyond by the end of 2022. The partnership operates through a coordination mechanism that aligns the Quad’s bilateral pledges with the COVAX Facility’s allocation framework, ensuring that doses are counted against COVAX’s fair‑share targets rather than creating parallel distribution channels.

Manufacturing capacity was anchored in four hubs: the Serum Institute of India (SII) and Biological E in India, the US‑based Novavax‑partnered facilities, Japan’s Takeda‑licensed production lines, and Australia’s CSL‑Seqirus network. By September 2022 the QVP had facilitated the release of approximately 720 million doses, of which 480 million were channelled through COVAX. The 2023 Quad Leaders’ Summit in Delhi (23‑24 September 2023) produced three concrete deliverables: (1) a renewed pledge of an additional 200 million doses for 2024‑2025, with a focus on bivalent and variant‑adapted vaccines; (2) the establishment of a Quad Vaccine Supply Chain Working Group tasked with mapping critical inputs — lipid nanoparticles, adjuvants, cold‑chain equipment — and identifying diversification strategies; and (3) a commitment to co‑finance a regional mRNA technology transfer hub in South‑East Asia, with an initial US$150 million seed fund contributed equally by the four Quad members.

The Delhi Summit also mandated a joint monitoring framework that reports quarterly to the Quad Senior Officials Meeting. The first monitoring report, released in January 2024, indicated that 85 % of the 2023‑2024 dose pledge had been contracted, and that the supply‑chain working group had identified 12 single‑source bottlenecks, of which three had been resolved through alternative sourcing agreements with manufacturers in the Republic of Korea and the European Union. The QVP’s integration with COVAX is governed by a Memorandum of Understanding signed in June 2022, which stipulates that all Quad‑financed doses are reported to the COVAX Allocation Mechanism within 48 hours of release, preserving transparency and avoiding double‑counting.

  • Confusing the PBF’s Immediate Response Facility with the Peacebuilding and Recovery Facility; the IRF has a 30‑day disbursement ceiling, the PRF operates on a 12‑month programme cycle.
  • Assuming the World Bank’s Climate Co‑Benefits coefficients are static; they are revised annually based on portfolio performance data.
  • Treating the ITLOS advisory opinion as a binding judgment; it is authoritative but non‑binding, unlike contentious case judgments.
  • Believing the Quad Vaccine Partnership replaces COVAX; it supplements COVAX and reports all doses through the COVAX Allocation Mechanism.
  • Overlooking that the PBF’s Results‑Based Financing pilot only covers 40 % of the approved envelope contingent on verification.
  • Misstating the IDA20 Climate Window amount; it is US$12 billion, not the total IDA20 envelope.
  • Aspirants should verify the latest ITLOS advisory opinion text before citing its legal effect.

WTO Investment Facilitation for Development Agreement: Text, Scope, and Developing‑Country Flexibilities

The Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD) Agreement was finalised in July 2024 after five years of negotiations under a Joint Statement Initiative (JSI) involving 127 WTO members. Unlike the failed Multilateral Agreement on Investment (1998) or the aborted Investment Facilitation Framework (2017), the IFD Agreement does not address market access, investment protection, or investor‑state dispute settlement (ISDS). Its scope is strictly procedural: transparency of investment measures, streamlining of administrative procedures, international cooperation, and sustainable investment promotion. The text comprises 22 articles and two annexes. Article 3 requires each participant to publish all investment‑related laws, regulations, and procedures in a single, publicly accessible online portal. Article 5 mandates the establishment of a single‑window mechanism or equivalent coordination platform for investment authorisations. Article 7 introduces a “reasonable timeframe” standard for processing applications, with a rebuttable presumption that 90 days is reasonable for standard projects and 180 days for complex ones. Article 11 creates a Committee on Investment Facilitation to monitor implementation and review the agreement every three years.

Developing‑country flexibilities are embedded throughout. Article 14 allows developing‑country participants to delay implementation of specific provisions for up to five years after entry into force, with least‑developed countries (LDCs) eligible for a seven‑year transition. Article 15 establishes a Technical Assistance and Capacity‑Building Facility, financed through voluntary contributions, with a target of US$50 million for the first triennium. The agreement enters into force once two‑thirds of participants have deposited instruments of acceptance; as of October 2024, 42 members had done so. Critically, the IFD Agreement applies on a most‑favoured‑nation (MFN) basis to all WTO members, not only participants, a design choice intended to avoid fragmentation but which raises free‑rider concerns. India and South Africa have not joined the JSI, arguing that investment facilitation encroaches on policy space reserved for the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and that the MFN extension undermines the principle of reciprocity. The agreement’s relationship with existing bilateral investment treaties (BITs) is addressed in Article 20: IFD commitments prevail only to the extent they are more favourable to the investor, preserving stricter BIT standards.

UN Peacekeeping Performance and Accountability: The Comprehensive Planning and Performance Assessment System (CPAS) and the Uniformed Capability Requirements

The Comprehensive Planning and Performance Assessment System (CPAS), launched in 2018 and fully rolled out across all multidimensional missions by 2021, represents the most systematic attempt to link mandate implementation to resource allocation in UN peacekeeping. CPAS operates on a three‑tier logic: (1) mission‑level results frameworks derived from Security Council resolutions, (2) component‑level performance indicators for military, police, and civilian pillars, and (3) unit‑level assessments using the Uniformed Capability Requirements (UCR) matrix. The UCR matrix, updated annually by the Department of Peace Operations (DPO), specifies minimum personnel, equipment, and training standards for each troop/police‑contributing country (T/PCC) pledge. For example, an infantry battalion deployed to MINUSCA must field 750 personnel with 85 % medical self‑sufficiency, Level 2+ hospital capability within 4 hours, and demonstrated proficiency in civilian protection tasks assessed through the Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System (PCRS). Performance data flows monthly into the CPAS dashboard, which generates a “traffic‑light” rating (green, amber, red) for each mandate task. Missions scoring red on two or more critical tasks for consecutive quarters trigger a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) negotiated between DPO, the mission leadership, and the relevant T/PCCs.

The accountability architecture includes three enforcement levers. First, the Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System (PCRS) ties reimbursement eligibility to UCR compliance: units failing the pre‑deployment assessment are placed in “conditional” status and receive only 80 % of the standard reimbursement rate until deficiencies are rectified.
