A question asks: “Which WTO body is the primary forum for discussing the compatibility of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism with WTO rules?” Options: (a) Dispute Settlement Body, (b) Committee on Trade and Environment, (c) Committee on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, (d) Trade Policy Review Body.
The correct answer is (b) Committee on Trade and Environment. The CTE’s mandate explicitly covers the trade impact of environmental policies and has been the venue where members have raised CBAM concerns since 2021. The Dispute Settlement Body would only be seized if a formal complaint were filed; the SCM Committee deals with subsidies, not border carbon measures; the Trade Policy Review Body conducts periodic peer reviews, not issue‑specific negotiations.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a new climate‑trade measure (CBAM, carbon clubs, green subsidies) to a WTO forum, default to the Committee on Trade and Environment unless the stem mentions a formal dispute or a specific agreement (SCM, TBT, GATT Art. XX). Remember that the CTE has no decision‑making power; its outputs are reports and recommendations, which examiners often test as “non‑binding dialogue”.

The G20 Energy Transitions Working Group: Hydrogen, Critical Minerals, and the 2023 Delhi Summit Deliverables

The G20 Energy Transitions Working Group (ETWG) was established under the Saudi presidency in 2020 and formally institutionalised during the Italian presidency in 2021. Its mandate is to coordinate G20 actions on clean‑energy deployment, energy‑efficiency, and the phase‑down of unabated fossil fuels, while ensuring energy security and affordability. The ETWG reports to the G20 Energy Ministers and feeds into the Leaders’ Summit communiqué.

Under the Indian presidency (2023), the ETWG prioritised three pillars: (1) a Global Hydrogen Initiative to harmonise standards, certification, and trade rules for low‑carbon hydrogen; (2) a Critical Minerals Mapping Exercise to identify supply‑risk hotspots for lithium, cobalt, rare‑earth elements, and copper, and to promote responsible mining practices aligned with the OECD Due Diligence Guidance; and (3) a Renewable Energy Capacity Target of tripling global installed renewable capacity to 11 TW by 2030, echoing the IEA’s Net‑Zero Roadmap.

The 2023 Delhi Summit delivered concrete outcomes: (a) the “G20 Hydrogen Declaration” endorsing a common methodology for carbon‑intensity accounting and inviting the International Partnership for Hydrogen and Fuel Cells in the Economy (IPHE) to develop a mutual‑recognition framework; (b) the “Critical Minerals Report” produced in collaboration with the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the World Bank, which identified 16 high‑risk minerals and recommended strategic stockpiling, recycling incentives, and investment in alternative chemistries; (c) a commitment to mobilise USD 100 billion annually for clean‑energy investment in emerging economies, operationalised through the G20‑backed Climate Finance Leadership Initiative. The ETWG also agreed to a biennial “Energy Transition Progress Report” to track implementation, with the first edition due in 2025.

The BRICS Science, Technology and Innovation Cooperation Framework: Joint Research Centres, Digital Economy, and the 2023 Johannesburg Summit Outcomes

Science, technology and innovation (STI) cooperation has been a standing agenda item since the first BRICS summit in 2009, but it gained a formal architecture at the 2023 Johannesburg Summit. Leaders adopted the “BRICS STI Cooperation Framework” establishing a permanent BRICS STI Committee co‑chaired by the science ministers of the rotating chair and the incoming chair. The Framework mandates three flagship programmes:

  • Joint Research Centres (JRCs): Five virtual centres were launched in 2024 focusing on artificial intelligence (hosted by China), biotechnology and health (hosted by Brazil), advanced materials (hosted by Russia), renewable energy integration (hosted by India), and quantum technologies (hosted by South Africa). Each JRC operates on a cost‑share basis, with funding contributions proportional to the member’s GDP (PPP).
  • Digital Economy Partnership: A BRICS Digital Economy Working Group was upgraded to a standing body tasked with developing interoperable data‑governance standards, cross‑border e‑payment interoperability (linking the BRICS Payment System), and a joint cyber‑security exercise calendar.
  • Talent Mobility Scheme: A short‑term researcher exchange programme targeting 500 fellows per year, with visa facilitation agreements signed by all five members in 2024.

The Framework also created a BRICS STI Fund, capitalised at USD 2 billion (initial pledges: China USD 800 million, India USD 500 million, Russia USD 300 million, Brazil USD 250 million, South Africa USD 150 million). The Fund finances JRC projects, joint patent pools, and the talent mobility scheme. Governance rests with a Board of Governors comprising the five science ministers and an independent Secretariat based in Beijing. The 2023 Summit declared that the STI Framework would be reviewed at the 2025 summit in Kazan, with an emphasis on measurable outputs such as co‑authored publications, joint patents, and commercialised prototypes.

The Quad Vaccine Partnership and Health Security Architecture: COVAX Coordination, Regional Production, and the 2023 Outcomes

The Quad Vaccine Partnership (QVP) was announced at the first Quad Leaders’ Summit in March 2021 as a practical pillar of the Quad’s “positive agenda”. Its objective is to expand safe, effective, and affordable COVID‑19 vaccine supply across the Indo‑Pacific, leveraging the manufacturing capacity of India, the financing and regulatory expertise of the United States, Japan, and Australia, and the distribution networks of COVAX. The partnership operates through a Quad Vaccine Working Group (QVWG) that meets quarterly and reports to the Quad Senior Officials Meeting.

Key milestones include: (1) the 2021 pledge to deliver 1 billion vaccine doses by end‑2022, of which approximately 720 million were shipped, primarily from India’s Serum Institute and Biological E; (2) the 2022 Quad Leaders’ Summit in Tokyo, where leaders committed to establishing a “Quad Regional Vaccine Production Hub” in India, with co‑financing from the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), and Export Finance Australia (EFA); (3) the 2023 Quad Leaders’ Summit in Hiroshima, which announced the operationalisation of the hub — two fill‑finish lines at Bharat Biotech and one at Indian Immunologicals — and a joint regulatory harmonisation initiative with the WHO Prequalification Programme to accelerate emergency‑use listing for new variant‑adapted vaccines.

Beyond COVID‑19, the QVP has broadened into a Quad Health Security Architecture (QHSA) encompassing: (a) a Quad Pandemic Preparedness Fund (initial capital USD 300 million) to finance early‑stage R&D for pathogen‑agnostic platforms; (b) a joint surveillance network linking the Indian Council of Medical Research, the US CDC, Japan’s National Institute of Infectious Diseases, and Australia’s Doherty Institute; and (c) a capacity‑building programme for ASEAN and Pacific Island countries on cold‑chain logistics, regulatory convergence, and vaccine confidence communication. The 2023 outcomes demonstrate a shift from ad‑hoc dose sharing to institutionalised production and regulatory cooperation, positioning the Quad as a complementary pillar to the WHO‑led global health architecture.

  • Confusing the HRC’s Universal Periodic Review with the treaty‑body reporting cycle — the UPR is a peer‑review, not a treaty‑monitoring mechanism.
  • Assuming the WTO Committee on Trade and Environment can adopt binding decisions; it only produces reports and recommendations.
  • Treating the G20 Energy Transitions Working Group as a formal treaty‑based body; it is an informal working group with no legal personality.
  • Believing the BRICS STI Fund operates like the New Development Bank; it is a project‑financing facility without lending windows.
  • Equating the Quad Vaccine Partnership with COVAX governance; the QVP is a bilateral‑plus coordination mechanism, not a multilateral allocation platform.
  • Overstating the legal force of the G20 Hydrogen Declaration; it is a political commitment, not a WTO‑compatible standard.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the HRC’s Special Procedures (independent experts) and the OHCHR’s country offices (UN staff).

These advanced sections equip you to dissect institutional mechanics, differentiate binding from non‑binding outputs, and anticipate examiner twists on emerging governance frameworks.

The United Nations Global Compact for Migration: Governance Structure, Implementation Review, and the International Migration Review Forum

The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM) was adopted by consensus at the Intergovernmental Conference in Marrakech on 10 December 2018 and subsequently endorsed by the UN General Assembly in Resolution 73/195. Although non‑legally binding, the Compact establishes a cooperative framework of 23 objectives covering the entire migration cycle, from drivers and departure to return and reintegration. Governance rests on three pillars: the UN Network on Migration, the Capacity‑Building Mechanism, and the follow‑up and review architecture.

UN Network on Migration

Established in 2018, the Network comprises 38 UN system entities, co‑chaired by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA). It coordinates technical assistance, data collection, and policy guidance. The Network’s Executive Committee meets quarterly; its Workplan 2022‑2024 prioritises mainstreaming migration into national development plans, strengthening consular protection, and improving migrant‑worker rights.

Capacity‑Building Mechanism

The Mechanism operates through a Multi‑Partner Trust Fund (MPTF) administered by the UN Multi‑Partner Trust Fund Office. As of 2023, the Fund had received pledges of USD 1.2 billion, with major contributions from the European Union, Germany, Canada, and the United States. Projects focus on border management, labour‑market integration, and diaspora engagement. Implementation is monitored through a results‑based framework with quarterly reporting to the Network.

Follow‑up and Review: International Migration Review Forum (IMRF)

The GCM mandates a state‑led review every four years through the International Migration Review Forum. The first IMRF convened in New York from 17‑20 May 2022, attended by 152 member states and over 300 stakeholders. The Forum adopted a Progress Declaration that identified gaps in data disaggregation, protection of migrant children, and access to social protection. The second IMRF is scheduled for 2026. In the interim, the UN General Assembly holds an annual informal interactive dialogue (the “High‑Level Dialogue on International Migration and Development”) to maintain political momentum.

Implementation Challenges

Key challenges include the voluntary nature of commitments, uneven national reporting (only 68 % of states submitted voluntary national reports by 2023), and limited financing for low‑income countries. The 2022 Progress Declaration called for a “whole‑of‑government” approach, stronger parliamentary oversight, and the integration of migration indicators into the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) monitoring framework.

The World Trade Organization Joint Initiative on Trade and Gender: Negotiating Dynamics, Developing Country Positions, and the 2023 Ministerial Outcomes

At the 12th Ministerial Conference (MC12) in Geneva, June 2022, a group of 71 WTO members launched the Joint Initiative on Trade and Gender (JITG). The initiative aims to identify how trade rules and policies can advance gender equality, building on the 2017 Buenos Aires Declaration on Women and Trade. The JITG operates as a plurilateral, open‑ended working group reporting to the General Council.

Negotiating Structure

The JITG is co‑chaired by Canada and Kenya, with a secretariat provided by the WTO Trade and Gender Unit. Its work programme comprises three pillars: (1) data and analysis — developing a gender‑disaggregated trade statistics framework; (2) policy tools — compiling best practices on gender‑responsive trade agreements; (3) capacity building — technical assistance for developing members to conduct gender impact assessments. Decisions are taken by consensus among participants; non‑participants are not bound by outcomes.

Developing Country Concerns

Many developing members, notably India, South Africa, and the African Group, have stressed that the initiative must not create new conditionalities for market access or impose prescriptive standards. They argue for flexibility in implementation, recognition of differing national legal frameworks, and the avoidance of “gender‑washing” in trade negotiations. The 2023 General Council meeting in December noted these concerns and agreed that any future outcomes would be voluntary and non‑binding.

2023 Outcomes

By the end of 2023, the JITG had produced a Stocktaking Report summarising 42 national case studies, a Gender‑Responsive Trade Policy Toolkit, and a set of Recommendations for the Committee on Trade and Development. The 2023 Ministerial Decision (adopted at the 13th Ministerial Conference in Abu Dhabi, February 2024) welcomed the progress, mandated the continuation of the work programme through 2025, and invited members to pilot the toolkit in at least two regional trade agreements. No legally binding text was adopted.

Technique: Distinguishing Plurilateral Initiatives from Multilateral Agreements
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the WTO Joint Initiative on Trade and Gender is correct? (a) It creates binding obligations for all WTO members. (b) It is a plurilateral initiative open to all members but only participants are bound by its outcomes. (c) It amends the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) 1994. (d) It establishes a new dispute‑settlement mechanism for gender‑related trade disputes.”
The correct answer is (b). The JITG is a plurilateral, voluntary initiative launched at MC12. Only participating members engage in its work programme, and any outputs (toolkit, recommendations) are non‑binding and do not amend covered agreements. It does not create a separate dispute‑settlement mechanism. Understanding the distinction between plurilateral initiatives (open, voluntary, non‑binding) and multilateral agreements (consensus‑based, binding on all members) is essential for answering such questions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question references a “Joint Initiative” or “Plurilateral” at the WTO, immediately flag it as voluntary and non‑binding unless the stem explicitly says “agreed to incorporate into Annex 1”. Look for keywords: “open‑ended”, “consensus among participants”, “voluntary toolkit”. These signal that the outcome does not create legal obligations for non‑participants.

The United Nations High‑Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development: Voluntary National Reviews, Thematic Reviews, and the 2023 SDG Summit

The High‑Level Political Forum (HLPF) is the UN’s central platform for follow‑up and review of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Established by General Assembly Resolution 67/290 (2013), it meets annually under the auspices of the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) and every four years at the level of Heads of State and Government under the General Assembly (the “SDG Summit”).

Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs)

VNRs are state‑led presentations of national progress on the SDGs. Since 2016, 187 countries have conducted at least one VNR; 44 presented in 2023. The reviews follow a common reporting guideline updated in 2022, emphasising data disaggregation, leave‑no‑one‑behind analysis, and integration of the “means of implementation” (finance, technology, capacity building). The HLPF’s VNR sessions include interactive dialogues with major groups and other stakeholders.

Thematic Reviews

Each HLPF cycle selects a set of SDGs for in‑depth thematic review. The 2023 cycle focused on SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals). Thematic reports are prepared by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs in collaboration with relevant specialised agencies.

2023 SDG Summit

The second SDG Summit convened on 18‑19 September 2023 in New York, marking the midpoint of the 2030 Agenda. The Summit adopted a Political Declaration (A/RES/78/1) that reaffirmed commitment to the SDGs, recognised the “polycrisis” of climate change, conflict, and COVID‑19, and called for a “Rescue Plan” comprising scaled‑up financing, debt relief for vulnerable countries, and a reform of the international financial architecture. The Declaration also mandated the Secretary‑General to present a “Global Sustainable Development Report” every two years, starting in 2024.

Governance and Accountability Gaps

Despite its inclusivity, the HLPF lacks enforcement mechanisms. VNRs are voluntary, thematic reviews are advisory, and the Political Declaration is non‑binding. Civil society organisations have criticised the limited speaking time for major groups and the absence of a formal follow‑up on Summit commitments. The 2023 Declaration attempted to address this by requesting ECOSOC to strengthen the HLPF’s working methods, including a more structured peer‑review process for VNRs.

The International Labour Organization Decent Work Agenda: The 2022 Global Call to Action, Social Protection Floors, and the Future of Work

The ILO’s Decent Work Agenda, articulated in the 1999 Director‑General’s Report and embedded in the 2008 Declaration on Social Justice for a Fair Globalisation, rests on four strategic pillars: employment creation, social protection, rights at work, and social dialogue. The 110th International Labour Conference (ILC) in June 2022 adopted a landmark “Global Call to Action for a Human‑Centred Recovery” (Resolution I), responding to the compounded impacts of the COVID‑19 pandemic, rising inequality, and climate change.

2022 Global Call to Action

The Call to Action urges member states to: (1) invest in inclusive, sustainable job creation, targeting youth, women, and informal workers; (2) extend universal social protection floors in line with Recommendation No. 202 (2012); (3) strengthen fundamental principles and rights at work, including freedom of association and collective bargaining; (4) promote social dialogue as a governance tool for recovery policies. The resolution also mandated the ILO Director‑General to report on implementation at the 111th ILC (2023).

Social Protection Floors

Recommendation No. 202 defines nationally defined social protection floors comprising basic income security for children, working‑age persons, and older persons, plus essential health care. As of 2023, 71 countries had adopted legislation or policy frameworks aligned with the Recommendation. The ILO’s “World Social Protection Report 2023” estimates that 4.1 billion people remain uncovered by any social protection benefit.

Future of Work

The ILO Centenary Declaration (2019) and the 2021 “Global Commission on the Future of Work” report frame the future‑of‑work agenda around three pillars: (a) investing in people’s capabilities through lifelong learning; (b) strengthening institutions of work, including labour standards for platform workers; (c) promoting decent and sustainable work in the green and digital transitions. The 2022 Call to Action reinforced these pillars by urging the development of a “Global Skills Partnership” and the adoption of a “Just Transition” framework for climate‑related labour market shifts.

Implementation Monitoring

The ILO’s supervisory system — Committee of Experts on the Application of Conventions and Recommendations (CEACR) and the Conference Committee on the Application of Standards — monitors compliance with ratified conventions. The 2022 Call to Action is not a convention; its implementation is tracked through voluntary national reporting to the ILC and through the ILO’s “Decent Work Country Programmes”.

The UN Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System: Force Generation, Performance Standards, and the 2023 Reform

The Peacekeeping Capability Readiness System (PCRS) was launched in 2017 as part of the “Action for Peacekeeping” (A4P) initiative to improve the predictability, quality, and timeliness of troop and police contributions. It replaces the ad‑hoc force‑generation process with a structured pipeline comprising three tiers: the Peacekeeping Capability Register (PCR), the Rapid Deployment Level (RDL), and the Strategic Deployment Level (SDL).

Peacekeeping Capability Register

The PCR is a voluntary, online database where troop‑contributing countries (TCCs) and police‑contributing countries (PCCs) register pledged units with detailed capability data — personnel strength, equipment, training status, and language proficiency. As of December 2023, 112 member states had registered 1,842 units. The Register enables the Department of Peace Operations (DPO) to match mission requirements with available capabilities in real time.

Rapid Deployment Level

Units at the RDL commit to deploy within 60 days of a request. To qualify, units must meet the “UN Peacekeeping Performance Standards” (adopted 2018, revised 2022), which cover operational readiness, conduct and discipline, gender parity (minimum 15 % women in formed units), and environmental management. The 2022 revision added a mandatory pre‑deployment assessment by the Integrated Training Service.

Strategic Deployment Level

The SDL comprises high‑capability units (e.g., engineering, aviation, medical) that can be deployed within 30 days for surge requirements. Participation requires a bilateral Memorandum of Understanding with the UN, including cost‑reimbursement arrangements and liability provisions.

2023 Reform: Action for Peacekeeping Plus (A4P+)

In March 2023, the Secretary‑General launched A4P+, a two‑year implementation plan addressing gaps identified in the 2022 PCRS review. Key measures include: (1) a new “Performance Accountability Framework” linking reimbursement rates to performance scores; (2) mandatory annual “Capability Validation Exercises” for RDL units; (3) a “Gender‑Responsive Deployment Target” raising the women‑in‑formed‑units goal to 25 % by 2025; (4) enhanced digital tools for real‑time capability tracking, including a mobile app for TCC focal points. The reform also established a “PCRS Oversight Board” co‑chaired by the Under‑Secretary‑General for Peace Operations and a rotating TCC representative.

Challenges

Despite progress, only 38 % of registered units meet RDL criteria, and deployment timelines average 95 days. Financing constraints, divergent national training standards, and political sensitivities around conditional reimbursement remain obstacles. The 2023 A4P+ review will report to the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations (C‑34) in 2025.

  • Confusing the voluntary nature of the Global Compact for Migration with binding treaty obligations — the GCM creates no legal duties.
  • Assuming the WTO Joint Initiative on Trade and Gender produces binding amendments to covered agreements — it yields only voluntary toolkits and recommendations.
  • Treating the HLPF’s Voluntary National Reviews as mandatory reporting with sanctions for non‑compliance — they are peer‑review exercises without enforcement.
  • Equating the ILO’s 2022 Global Call to Action with a new Convention — it is a resolution guiding policy, not a ratifiable instrument.
  • Believing the PCRS Rapid Deployment Level guarantees deployment within 60 days for all pledged units — only units that meet performance standards and pass validation qualify.
  • Overstating the legal force of the 2023 SDG Summit Political Declaration — it is a political commitment, not a legally binding treaty.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the UN Network on Migration (coordination body) and the International Migration Review Forum (state‑led review platform).

The advanced sections above provide the mechanistic detail and comparative nuance required to navigate complex institutional questions in the examination.

The United Nations Human Rights Council: Universal Periodic Review Mechanism, Special Procedures, and the 2023‑2024 Reform Debates

The Human Rights Council (HRC), established in 2006 by General Assembly resolution 60/251, replaced the Commission on Human Rights. Its flagship mechanism is the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), a state‑driven process that examines the human rights records of all 193 UN member states every 4.5 years. Each review cycle comprises three stages: (1) submission of a national report, a compilation of UN information, and a summary of stakeholder submissions; (2) an interactive dialogue in the UPR Working Group where any member state may pose questions and make recommendations; (3) adoption of an outcome report containing accepted and noted recommendations, followed by a voluntary mid‑term implementation update.

Complementing the UPR are the Special Procedures — independent experts, special rapporteurs, and working groups mandated to address thematic or country‑specific issues. As of 2024 there are 45 thematic mandates (e.g., freedom of expression, torture, climate change) and 13 country mandates. Mandate holders conduct country visits, send communications to states, and present annual reports to the HRC and the General Assembly. Their findings are non‑binding but carry significant normative weight and often trigger diplomatic engagement.

Since the 2023 session, the Council has intensified debates on reforming the UPR to enhance effectiveness. Key proposals include: (a) extending the review cycle to five years to allow deeper analysis; (b) introducing a “focus‑area” approach where each cycle prioritises a cluster of rights (e.g., economic, social and cultural rights) to avoid superficial coverage; (c) strengthening the follow‑up mechanism by requiring states to submit a concrete implementation matrix within 12 months of adoption; (d) improving the participation of national human rights institutions (NHRIs) and civil society through accredited speaking slots. The 2024 HRC resolution 55/12 endorsed a pilot “enhanced follow‑up” for 12 volunteer states, with an evaluation scheduled for the 2026 session.

Critics argue that the UPR’s consensus‑based adoption allows states to water down recommendations, while the Special Procedures face access denials and reprisals against cooperating individuals. The Council’s membership, elected by regional groups, has periodically included states with poor rights records, prompting calls for competitive elections and objective criteria. The 2023‑2024 reform track reflects a broader push to align the HRC’s working methods with the 2030 Agenda’s pledge to leave no one behind.

The International Maritime Organization: Polar Code Implementation, GHG Reduction Strategy, and the 2023 Revised Strategy

The International Maritime Organization (IMO), a specialised UN agency with 175 member states, regulates shipping safety, security, and environmental performance. Two recent regulatory frameworks dominate its agenda: the Polar Code and the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Reduction Strategy.

The International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters (Polar Code) entered into force on 1 January 2017 under the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL). It sets mandatory standards for ship design, construction, equipment, operations, training, and environmental protection for vessels navigating Arctic and Antarctic waters. Implementation is monitored through flag‑state surveys and port‑state control inspections. As of 2023, 68 flag states had reported full compliance for their polar‑class fleets, while gaps persist in crew certification and ice‑navigator training.

The Initial IMO GHG Strategy, adopted in 2018 (MEPC.304(72)), set a vision to reduce total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 50 % by 2050 compared with 2008, and to pursue efforts towards phasing them out. The 2023 Revised Strategy (MEPC.377(80)), adopted at the 80th session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee, raises ambition: (i) carbon intensity of international shipping to decline by at least 40 % by 2030; (ii) uptake of zero‑or‑near‑zero GHG technologies, fuels, or energy sources to represent at least 5 % (striving for 10 %) of the energy used by 2030; (iii) net‑zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. The revision also introduces a “basket of candidate mid‑term measures” — a technical element (a goal‑based fuel standard) and an economic element (a carbon pricing mechanism) — to be finalised by 2025 for entry into force in 2027.

Developing states, particularly small island developing states (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs), have emphasised the need for capacity‑building, technology transfer, and a just transition fund. The IMO’s Technical Cooperation Committee oversees the “IMO‑GHG TC Trust Fund” to support these needs. Meanwhile, the Polar Code’s environmental chapter (Chapter 4) aligns with the GHG Strategy by requiring ships to carry a Polar Water Operational Manual that includes emission‑reduction planning for polar voyages.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which IMO instrument sets mandatory design and equipment standards for ships operating in Arctic waters, and what is the target year for net‑zero GHG emissions from international shipping under the 2023 Revised Strategy?"
The Polar Code (adopted under SOLAS and MARPOL) establishes mandatory design, equipment, and operational standards for polar navigation. The 2023 Revised GHG Strategy sets a target of net‑zero GHG emissions from international shipping by or around 2050.
Exam‑day strategy
When comparing IMO instruments, link the Polar Code to safety and pollution prevention (SOLAS/MARPOL) and the GHG Strategy to climate ambition. Remember the 2023 Revised Strategy’s three quantitative targets (2030 carbon intensity, 2030 zero‑carbon fuel uptake, 2050 net‑zero) — they are frequent MCQ anchors.

The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction: Sendai Framework Mid‑Term Review, the 2023 Political Declaration, and Monitoring Gaps

The UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) serves as the focal point for the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015‑2030, adopted at the Third UN World Conference in Sendai, Japan. The Framework outlines four priorities for action and seven global targets (A‑G) to be achieved by 2030, including substantial reductions in disaster mortality, affected populations, economic losses, and damage to critical infrastructure.

The mid‑term review, mandated by General Assembly resolution 75/216, culminated in the High‑Level Meeting of the General Assembly on 18‑19 May 2023. The resulting Political Declaration (A/RES/77/289) reaffirmed commitment to the seven targets and highlighted three systemic gaps: (1) insufficient integration of disaster risk reduction (DRR) into national development planning and climate adaptation strategies; (2) chronic under‑investment in pre‑disaster resilience, with only 4.5 % of official development assistance (ODA) allocated to DRR in 2022; (3) data deficiencies — 62 % of member states lack comprehensive disaster loss databases aligned with the Sendai Monitor indicators.

To address these gaps, the Declaration calls for: (a) a “Sendai Framework Accelerator” to mobilise technical assistance for national DRR strategies; (b) the establishment of a global partnership for disaster‑related data, leveraging the UN Statistical Commission’s work on the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA); (c) enhanced engagement of local governments through the “Making Cities Resilient 2030” initiative, which now counts 1,200 participating cities. The UNDRR’s 2023‑2025 work programme prioritises the development of a “Global Risk Assessment Framework” to standardise probabilistic risk modelling across sectors.

Monitoring remains voluntary; states report through the Sendai Framework Monitor, an online platform launched in 2018. As of December 2023, 115 countries had submitted at least one national progress report. The 2024 Global Assessment Report (GAR) will synthesize these inputs and provide the first comprehensive mid‑term snapshot of target trajectories.

The International Atomic Energy Agency: Convention on Nuclear Safety Review Process, the 2023 Extraordinary Meeting, and Emerging Safety Challenges

The IAEA, with 176 member states, administers the Convention on Nuclear Safety (CNS), a legally binding instrument that entered into force in 1996. The CNS obliges parties to maintain a legislative and regulatory framework for nuclear installations, conduct safety assessments, and submit national reports for peer review at triennial Review Meetings. The 8th Review Meeting was held in Vienna in March‑April 2023, preceded by an Extraordinary Meeting in June 2022 prompted by the conflict in Ukraine and the safety implications for the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.

The 2023 Review Meeting adopted a “Vienna Declaration on Nuclear Safety” that emphasises: (i) strengthening the safety culture and leadership for safety; (ii) enhancing the effectiveness of the peer‑review process through more transparent country‑specific findings; (iii) addressing the safety of nuclear facilities in armed conflict, including the principle of “non‑targeting” and the need for robust off‑site emergency preparedness. The Declaration also encourages parties to ratify the Joint Convention on the Safety of Spent Fuel Management and on the Safety of Radioactive Waste Management, which held its 7th Review Meeting in 2022.

Emerging challenges discussed include: the deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs) and their licensing frameworks; cyber threats to instrumentation and control systems; and the long‑term management of radioactive waste from decommissioning. The IAEA’s “Safety Standards Series” is being updated to incorporate SMR‑specific guidance (e.g., SSG‑71 on “Safety of Small Modular Reactors”). The 9th Review Meeting is scheduled for 2026, with a preparatory “Topical Meeting on Safety of Nuclear Installations in Conflict Zones” planned for 2025.

The OECD Development Assistance Committee: 2023 Peer Review Cycle, the DAC Recommendation on Enabling Civil Society, and ODA Measurement Reforms

The OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) comprises 30 members that provide the bulk of global official development assistance (ODA). Its peer review mechanism, conducted on a four‑year cycle, assesses each member’s development co‑operation policies, institutional architecture, and results. The 2023 cycle reviewed Australia, Canada, the European Union, France, Germany, Japan, the Republic of Korea, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Common findings highlighted the need for: (a) stronger alignment with the 2030 Agenda and the Paris Agreement; (b) improved transparency and predictability of funding; (c) enhanced localisation — channelling resources through local actors.

In July 2022 the DAC adopted the Recommendation on Enabling Civil Society in Development Co‑operation and Humanitarian Assistance (OECD/LEGAL/0455). It sets out principles for protecting civic space, ensuring meaningful participation of civil society organisations (CSOs) in policy dialogue, and safeguarding them from undue restrictions. The 2023 peer reviews included a dedicated “civil society enablement” chapter, scoring members on legal frameworks, funding modalities, and consultation practices.

On ODA measurement, the DAC has advanced the Total Official Support for Sustainable Development (TOSSD) framework, which captures a broader set of resource flows — including private finance mobilised through official interventions, triangular co‑operation, and support to global public goods. The 2023 TOSSD reporting round saw 28 members submit data, covering 2021‑2022 flows. The DAC also refined the “grant‑equivalent” methodology for concessional loans, aligning discount rates with the IMF’s unified interest rate. These reforms aim to improve comparability and to reflect the evolving architecture of development finance beyond traditional ODA.

  • Confusing the UPR’s voluntary mid‑term update with a mandatory reporting obligation — the update is encouraged but not required.
  • Assuming the Polar Code applies to all ships globally — it only applies to vessels operating in defined Arctic and Antarctic waters.
  • Treating the Sendai Framework’s seven targets as legally binding — they are political commitments monitored through voluntary reporting.
  • Believing the CNS Review Meetings produce binding sanctions — they generate peer‑review findings and recommendations, not enforcement actions.
  • Equating TOSSD with ODA — TOSSD is a broader statistical framework that includes non‑concessional flows and private finance mobilised.
  • Overstating the legal force of the DAC Recommendation on Enabling Civil Society — it is a soft‑law instrument guiding members, not a treaty.

ITLOS Advisory Opinion on Climate Change (2023): Obligations under UNCLOS, the 1.5°C Standard, and Implications for the UNFCCC Regime

On 21 May 2024, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) delivered its landmark advisory opinion in the Request for an Advisory Opinion submitted by the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law (COSIS). This was the first authoritative judicial pronouncement by an international court or tribunal on the specific obligations of states under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) with respect to climate change and ocean acidification. The Tribunal, sitting as a full bench of 21 judges, unanimously concluded that anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions constitute pollution of the marine environment within the meaning of Article 1(1)(4) of UNCLOS, thereby triggering the due diligence obligations under Part XII (Protection and Preservation of the Marine Environment).

The opinion establishes several critical legal benchmarks. First, the Tribunal interpreted the obligation under Article 194(1) to take all necessary measures to prevent, reduce, and control marine pollution as requiring states to adopt legislation and regulations aligned with the best available science and the 1.5°C temperature goal of the Paris Agreement. The Tribunal explicitly stated that the standard of due diligence is not static but evolves with scientific knowledge, and that the global temperature goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels constitutes the relevant benchmark for assessing the adequacy of national measures. Second, the Tribunal clarified that the obligation under Article 194(2) to ensure that activities within a state’s jurisdiction or control do not cause damage by pollution to other states and their environment applies to GHG emissions, establishing a transboundary harm framework for climate change under the law of the sea. Third, the opinion addresses ocean acidification as a distinct pathway of harm, requiring states to monitor and mitigate CO₂ absorption by the oceans.

On the relationship between UNCLOS and the UNFCCC/Paris Agreement, the Tribunal adopted a mutual supportiveness approach. It held that the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement are the primary legal instruments for addressing climate change, but that UNCLOS Part XII obligations operate in parallel and are not displaced. Compliance with the Paris Agreement does not automatically satisfy UNCLOS due diligence obligations; rather, the specific stringency of Part XII — including the requirement to act on the basis of best available science and the 1.5°C threshold — may demand more rigorous action. The Tribunal also affirmed that the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) applies in the interpretation of UNCLOS obligations, but does not relieve any state of its due diligence duty. The opinion further elaborates on obligations for environmental impact assessment (Article 206), monitoring and reporting (Article 204), international cooperation (Article 197), and capacity building and technology transfer (Articles 202, 203) in the climate-ocean nexus.

The advisory opinion has immediate practical significance for the Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement, the development of new NDCs due in 2025, and ongoing negotiations on the BBNJ Agreement (marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction). It also strengthens the legal basis for future contentious cases before ITLOS, the ICJ, or arbitral tribunals under UNCLOS Annex VII. The Tribunal’s reasoning on the 1.5°C standard as a due diligence benchmark is likely to be cited in the pending ICJ advisory proceedings on climate obligations (requested by UNGA Resolution 77/276 in March 2023) and in the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion on climate emergency and human rights.

UNCITRAL Working Group III on ISDS Reform: The Multilateral Investment Court, the Mauritius Convention, and the Future of International Investment Agreements

The United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Working Group III (Investor-State Dispute Settlement Reform) has been the primary multilateral forum for addressing systemic concerns in the investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) system since its mandate was expanded in 2017. The reform agenda targets four core areas: consistency and coherence of arbitral awards, legitimacy and transparency, cost and duration of proceedings, and the adjudicator selection mechanism. After six years of intensive negotiations, the Working Group reached a critical juncture at its 45th session (New York, April–May 2024) with the presentation of a draft statute for a Multilateral Investment Court (MIC) as the centrepiece of a permanent appellate and first-instance mechanism to replace ad hoc arbitration under treaties such as the ICSID Convention and UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules.

The proposed MIC statute envisions a two-tier structure: a first-instance tribunal composed of 10–15 judges elected by member states for fixed terms, and an appellate tribunal of 7–9 judges. Judges would be required to meet strict independence, impartiality, and competence criteria, including a prohibition on acting as counsel or party-appointed expert in investment disputes during and for a cooling-off period after their tenure. The draft statute incorporates a code of conduct drawing on the 2021 UNCITRAL Model Rules for Investor-State Mediation and the IBA Guidelines on Conflicts of Interest. Decisions of the appellate tribunal would be binding and final, addressing the consistency deficit that has plagued the current system where different tribunals reach divergent conclusions on identical treaty provisions.

A parallel track concerns the Mauritius Convention on Transparency (entered into force 2017), which extends the UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency in Treaty-based Investor-State Arbitration to investment treaties concluded before 1 April 2014. As of mid-2024, the Convention has 11 parties (including Canada, Chile, Mauritius, and the EU), but major capital-exporting states such as the United States, Japan, and China have not joined. The Working Group is exploring whether transparency provisions — including public access to documents, open hearings, and third-party submissions — should be integrated directly into the MIC statute as default rules, thereby bypassing the need for universal ratification of the Mauritius Convention.

The reform dynamics are complicated by regional and bilateral developments. The EU’s Investment Court System (ICS), operationalised in CETA (Canada) and the EU-Vietnam FTA, serves as a de facto prototype for the first-instance tier, but its appellate mechanism remains underdeveloped. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Investment Protocol (adopted February 2023) incorporates a standing appellate body and excludes ISDS for a transition period, reflecting Global South preferences for state-centric dispute resolution. Meanwhile, the USMCA (2020) eliminated ISDS between the US and Canada and restricted it with Mexico to limited sectors, signalling a retreat from traditional ISDS by the largest capital exporter. The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) retains ISDS but with a code of conduct and appellate review mechanism under development.

The critical path forward hinges on the “opt-in” versus “mandatory” design of the MIC. Developing countries, led by the African Group and India, advocate for a mandatory system that applies automatically to all future IIAs and, via a protocol, to existing treaties. Developed countries, including the EU and Canada, prefer an opt-in mechanism that preserves party autonomy. The Working Group’s 46th session (October 2024) is expected to negotiate the transition clause for existing treaties — whether states can “opt out” of the MIC for legacy disputes, and how the MIC interacts with pending arbitrations. The outcome will determine whether the MIC becomes a universal court or a parallel forum coexisting with ICSID and ad hoc arbitration, fundamentally reshaping the enforcement architecture of international investment law.

Examiner's Trap: Confusing ITLOS Advisory Opinion with ICJ Advisory Proceedings
A question asks: "The 2024 ITLOS advisory opinion on climate change was requested by the UN General Assembly under Article 96 of the UN Charter." Identify the error and state the correct requesting body and legal basis.
The statement is incorrect. The ITLOS advisory opinion was requested by the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law (COSIS), an intergovernmental organisation, under Article 21 of the Statute of ITLOS (Annex VI to UNCLOS) read with Article 138 of the ITLOS Rules. The UN General Assembly requested a separate advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in March 2023 under Article 96 of the UN Charter and Article 65 of the ICJ Statute. The two proceedings are distinct in requesting body, legal basis, and tribunal.
Exam-Day Strategy: Mapping Advisory Opinions
Create a two-column table: ICJ Advisory Opinions (UNGA/UNSC request, UN Charter Art. 96) vs ITLOS Advisory Opinions (international organisation request per ITLOS Statute Art. 21). Note the 2023 ICJ request (climate obligations), 2024 ITLOS opinion (COSIS request, UNCLOS obligations), and 2023 ITLOS advisory opinion on IUU fishing (requested by COSIS). This distinction is a favourite UPSC trap in both Prelims and Mains.

Financial Stability Board: Governance Structure, Key Standards for Sound Financial Systems, and the Climate-Related Disclosure Framework under the ISSB

The Financial Stability Board (FSB), established in 2009 as the successor to the Financial Stability Forum, is the primary global body for coordinating financial regulation and supervisory standards across the G20 jurisdictions. Unlike the IMF or the Basel Committee, the FSB has no treaty basis; it operates as a voluntary, consensus-based body hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel. Its Plenary — comprising finance ministers, central bank governors, and heads of financial regulators from 24 jurisdictions plus the EU, plus international organisations (IMF, World Bank, BIS, OECD, IAIS, IOSCO, BCBS) — sets the strategic direction. The Steering Committee provides operational guidance between Plenary meetings, while Standing Committees (Assessment of Vulnerabilities, Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, Standards Implementation, Budget and Resources) execute the work programme.

The FSB’s core mandate is to promote the implementation of the Key Standards for Sound Financial Systems — a set of 14 international standards covering banking (Basel Core Principles), securities (IOSCO Objectives and Principles), insurance (IAIS Insurance Core Principles), financial market infrastructure (CPMI-IOSCO Principles for FMIs), transparency and accounting (IFRS, audit), corporate governance (G20/OECD Principles), deposit insurance (IADI Core Principles), and anti-money laundering (FATF Recommendations). The FSB conducts peer reviews of member jurisdictions’ implementation of these standards, publishing thematic and country-specific reports. The 2023 peer review cycle focused on cyber resilience and non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI), with findings highlighting data gaps in measuring leverage and liquidity transformation in money market funds, hedge funds, and private credit funds.

On climate-related financial risks, the FSB has been the architect of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), established in 2015 and chaired by Michael Bloomberg. The TCFD’s 2017 recommendations — structured around governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets — became the de facto global baseline for climate disclosure. In 2021, the FSB mandated the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) under the IFRS Foundation to develop a global baseline for sustainability disclosures, building on the TCFD framework. The ISSB issued its inaugural standards — IFRS S1 (General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information) and IFRS S2 (Climate-related Disclosures) — in June 2023, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024. The FSB’s 2023 progress report on Roadmap for Addressing Climate-Related Financial Risks tracks jurisdictional adoption: as of October 2023, 16 FSB jurisdictions had made TCFD-aligned disclosures mandatory or were in the process of doing so, including the UK, EU (via CSRD/ESRS), Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, and New Zealand. The US SEC’s climate disclosure rules (adopted March 2024, subsequently stayed pending litigation) represent a partial alignment.

The FSB’s 2024 work programme prioritises three climate-finance intersections: (1) transition planning — developing supervisory guidance on the credibility and implementation of financial institutions’ net-zero transition plans; (2) data and analytics — addressing the “greenium” measurement, scope 3 emissions data quality, and the use of scenario analysis in stress testing; and (3) vulnerabilities in NBFI — assessing how climate risks propagate through asset managers, insurers, and shadow banking channels. The FSB also coordinates with the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) — a coalition of 127 central banks and supervisors — on scenario design and supervisory practices. Critically, the FSB lacks enforcement power; its influence derives from G20 endorsement, peer pressure, and the incorporation of its standards into IMF Article IV surveillance and World Bank/IMF Financial Sector Assessment Programs (FSAPs). The 2024 FSB Plenary (October, Washington DC) will review the first ISSB implementation monitoring report and consider whether to expand the Key Standards to include sustainability disclosure as a 15th standard.

UN High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development: Voluntary National Review Mechanics, the 2023 SDG Summit Political Declaration, and the HLPF Reform Debate

The High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (HLPF), established by Rio+20 (2012) and formalised in UNGA Resolution 67/290, is the central UN platform for the follow-up and review of the 2030 Agenda. It meets annually under the auspices of ECOSOC for eight days (including a three-day ministerial segment) and every four years at the level of Heads of State and Government under the UN General Assembly (the SDG Summit). The HLPF’s review architecture rests on three pillars: Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs), thematic reviews of SDG clusters, and global reviews informed by the Secretary-General’s annual SDG Progress Report and the Global Sustainable Development Report (GSDR, quadrennial).

VNR Mechanics: Countries volunteer to present VNRs — 188 of 193 UN member states have presented at least once as of 2024. The VNR Handbook (updated 2023) prescribes a structured process: (i) national preparation involving whole-of-government and whole-of-society consultations; (ii) submission of a main report and executive summary to the UN Secretariat at least six weeks before the HLPF; (iii) a 30-minute presentation at the HLPF followed by a 30-minute interactive dialogue with member states, major groups, and other stakeholders; (iv) a written summary of the dialogue posted on the HLPF database. The 2023 guidelines introduced a “second-generation VNR” framework emphasising integration (policy coherence across SDGs), leave no one behind (disaggregated data), and institutionalisation (embedding SDGs in budget cycles and parliamentary oversight). A VNR Lab during the HLPF facilitates peer learning. However, VNRs remain voluntary, non-binding, and non-comparative — there is no scoring, ranking, or compliance mechanism.

The 2023 SDG Summit (18–19 September, New York) adopted the Political Declaration “Accelerating the implementation of the 2030 Agenda”. Key commitments include: (a) a SDG Stimulus of at least $500 billion per year in affordable long-term financing for developing countries, to be delivered through MDB reform, SDR rechanneling, and debt relief; (b) a recommitment to 0.7% ODA/GNI and 0.15–0.20% for LDCs; (c) reform of the international financial architecture including quota reform at the IMF and capital adequacy frameworks at MDBs; (d) strengthening the HLPF through “more focused, action-oriented, and inclusive reviews” and “enhanced follow-up on VNR recommendations.” The Declaration also mandated the UN Secretary-General to propose options for HLPF reform by the 2024 session.

The HLPF reform debate centres on four tensions: (1) Accountability vs Voluntariness — developing countries (G77) resist any “naming and shaming” or peer review with teeth; developed countries push for stronger follow-up mechanisms. (2) Integration vs Silos — the current thematic cluster approach (e.g., 2024: SDGs 1, 2, 13, 16, 17) is criticised for fragmenting the indivisible agenda. (3) Inclusivity vs Efficiency — Major Groups and Other Stakeholders (MGoS) demand guaranteed speaking slots; member states prioritise government-led dialogues. (4) Linkage with Financing for Development (FfD) Forum — the 2025 FfD Conference (Spain) and the 2027 SDG Summit require a coherent review architecture. The Secretary-General’s 2024 report (A/79/–) is expected to propose a “HLPF+” model with a standing bureau, multi-year thematic cycles, and a formal “VNR follow-up” mechanism — but consensus remains elusive.

International Civil Aviation Organization: CORSIA Phases, the 2022 Long-Term Aspirational Goal for Net-Zero 2050, and the 2024 Assembly Stocktaking

The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), a UN specialised agency with 193 member states, governs international aviation emissions through the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) — the first global market-based measure for any single sector. Adopted at the 39th Assembly (2016), CORSIA operates in three phases: Pilot Phase (2021–2023) — voluntary participation by states; Phase 1 (2024–2026) — voluntary; Phase 2 (2027–2035) — mandatory for all states except LDCs, SIDS, LLDCs, and states with <0.5% of international revenue tonne-kilometres (RTK) (unless they volunteer). As of January 2024, 126 states (representing ~97% of international aviation activity) volunteered for the Pilot Phase and Phase 1. The scheme covers international flights only; domestic aviation falls under national NDCs.

CORSIA’s baseline was originally the average of 2019–2020 emissions, but the 40th Assembly (2022) revised it to 2019 emissions only (85% of 2019 levels from 2024 onward) due to the COVID-19 distortion. Airlines must monitor, report, and verify (MRV) emissions annually using approved Emissions Monitoring Plans. Offsetting requirements are calculated at the sectoral level (not individual airline) for the Pilot Phase and Phase 1, shifting to a sectoral/individual hybrid (70/30) in Phase 2, and fully individual from 2030. Eligible Emissions Units (EEUs) are approved by the ICAO Council based on recommendations from the Technical Advisory Body (TAB); as of 2024, 14 programmes (including CDM, Gold Standard, Verra, ART) are eligible for the Pilot Phase, subject to vintage restrictions (post-2016). Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) and lower carbon aviation fuels (LCAF) can reduce offsetting obligations if certified under the CORSIA Sustainability Criteria (lifecycle emissions reduction ≥10%, no deforestation, safeguards).

The 41st Assembly (September–October 2022) adopted a historic Long-Term Aspirational Goal (LTAG) of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 for international aviation — aligning the sector with the Paris Agreement temperature goal. The LTAG is aspirational and collective, not legally binding on individual states or airlines. The Assembly requested the Council to develop a roadmap with intermediate milestones (2030, 2040) and to explore a global SAF framework. The 2024 ICAO Assembly (39th Session, September–October 2024) will conduct the first LTAG stocktaking, reviewing progress on: (i) SAF deployment — current production <0.2% of jet fuel demand; target 5% by 2030 per the CAAF/3 Declaration (Dubai, November 2023); (ii) aircraft technology — hydrogen and electric propulsion timelines; (iii) operational improvements — air traffic management modernisation; (iv) CORSIA integrity — EEU quality, double counting avoidance, and the Article 6 correspondence with host country NDCs. The Assembly will also consider CORSIA periodic review outcomes (first review due 2025) and the feasibility of a global levy as a complement to offsetting — a proposal championed by the International Air Transport Association (IATA) and several developing countries to generate predictable climate finance.

  • Common Trap: Conflating CORSIA’s offsetting mechanism with the EU ETS — CORSIA applies to international routes only and uses offsetting; the EU ETS covers intra-EEA flights and uses cap-and-trade with allowances. They operate in parallel with complex interaction rules.
  • Common Trap: Assuming the LTAG (net-zero 2050) is a legally binding target for each state — it is a collective aspirational goal adopted by Assembly Resolution A41-21, not a treaty obligation.
  • Common Trap: Confusing the FSB’s TCFD recommendations with the ISSB’s IFRS S1/S2 standards — TCFD was a voluntary framework (2017); ISSB standards are the new global baseline (2023) endorsed by IOSCO and the FSB for jurisdictional adoption.
  • Common Trap: Believing the Multilateral Investment Court (MIC) already exists — as of mid-2024, only a draft statute has been negotiated in UNCITRAL Working Group III; no treaty has been adopted, and the opt-in vs mandatory design remains unresolved.
  • Common Trap: Treating ITLOS and ICJ advisory opinions on climate change as the same proceeding — they were requested by different bodies (COSIS vs UNGA), under different statutes (ITLOS Statute Art. 21 vs UN Charter Art. 96), and address different primary legal regimes (UNCLOS vs UNFCCC/human rights).
  • Common Trap: Assuming VNRs at the HLPF are assessed or ranked — they are purely voluntary presentations with interactive dialogue; no scoring, compliance finding, or enforcement mechanism exists.
  • Common Trap: Equating the FSB with a treaty-based organisation — the FSB is a voluntary G20-hosted body with no legal personality; its standards are soft law implemented through peer review and IMF/World Bank FSAPs.

UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review: Mechanism, Cycles, and Implementation Gaps

The Universal Periodic Review (UPR) is a State‑driven peer review mechanism established by UN General Assembly resolution 60/251 (2006) and operationalised through Human Rights Council (HRC) resolution 5/1 (2007). Every UN member State undergoes a review every four and a half years; the first cycle ran 2008‑2011, the second 2012‑2016, the third 2017‑2021, and the fourth began in 2022. Each review consists of three documents: the national report prepared by the State under review, a compilation of UN treaty‑body and special‑procedure reports prepared by the OHCHR, and a summary of stakeholder submissions (NHRIs, NGOs). The interactive dialogue in the Working Group lasts three and a half hours, after which the troika (three rapporteur States) drafts a report containing recommendations. The reviewed State must indicate which recommendations it accepts, notes, or rejects; the outcome is adopted at a subsequent HRC plenary session.

Key procedural features include the principle of universality (all States reviewed), the cooperative nature (no adversarial prosecution), and the voluntary implementation of accepted recommendations. The OHCHR maintains a UPR database tracking acceptance rates; historically, States accept roughly 70‑80 % of recommendations, with higher acceptance for economic, social and cultural rights than for civil and political rights. The fourth cycle introduced a “mid‑term reporting” pilot, encouraging States to submit voluntary updates on implementation two years after adoption. However, the mechanism faces persistent gaps: limited follow‑up capacity at the national level, uneven civil‑society participation (especially in closed political environments), and the absence of a formal compliance enforcement tool. The HRC’s “UPR Voluntary Fund” and “Technical Assistance Trust Fund” aim to bridge capacity deficits, but funding remains donor‑dependent and unpredictable.

From an examiner’s perspective, the UPR is frequently contrasted with treaty‑body reporting: the UPR is political and peer‑based, whereas treaty bodies are legal and expert‑driven. Questions may ask about the role of the troika, the distinction between “accepted” and “noted” recommendations, or the significance of the 2022 “HRC resolution 48/13” which strengthened the follow‑up framework by requesting the OHCHR to prepare a matrix of implementation for each State. A common trap is to conflate the UPR’s outcome document with a legally binding decision; it remains a political commitment, not a judicial ruling.

ITLOS Advisory Opinion on Climate Change Obligations under UNCLOS: Request, Findings, and Legal Significance

In December 2022, the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law (COSIS) requested an advisory opinion from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) under Article 21 of the ITLOS Statute and Article 138 of UNCLOS. The request posed two core questions: (1) what are the specific obligations of State parties to prevent, reduce and control marine pollution from anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions; and (2) what are the obligations to protect and preserve the marine environment from climate change impacts, including ocean warming, acidification and sea‑level rise. The Tribunal delivered its opinion on 21 May 2024, constituting the first authoritative judicial pronouncement on the intersection of UNCLOS and climate change.

The opinion affirmed that greenhouse gas emissions constitute “pollution of the marine environment” within the meaning of Article 1(1)(4) of UNCLOS, thereby triggering the due‑diligence obligation under Article 194(1) to take all necessary measures to prevent, reduce and control such pollution. ITLOS clarified that the standard of due diligence is not static; it evolves with best available science and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR). The Tribunal held that States must adopt mitigation measures consistent with the 1.5 °C pathway of the Paris Agreement, and that failure to align national policies with that pathway may breach UNCLOS obligations. On adaptation, the opinion stressed the duty to cooperate through global and regional organisations, to conduct environmental impact assessments (EIAs) for activities with significant transboundary marine effects, and to provide assistance to vulnerable States, particularly SIDS.

Crucially, ITLOS declared that the obligations under UNCLOS are complementary to, not subordinate to, the UNFCCC regime. The Tribunal rejected the argument that UNFCCC lex specialis displaces UNCLOS, noting that UNCLOS provides a distinct legal basis for marine‑specific obligations. The opinion also addressed the contentious issue of “loss and damage”, stating that while UNCLOS does not create a standalone compensation mechanism, the duty to cooperate includes facilitating access to remedy for climate‑induced marine harm. The advisory opinion is non‑binding but carries significant normative weight; it is expected to influence future UNFCCC negotiations, national litigation, and the work of the International Law Commission on sea‑level rise.

Examiner's technique: Comparative legal reasoning
A question asks: “Distinguish the legal basis and enforceability of the ITLOS 2024 advisory opinion on climate change from the ICJ 2024 advisory opinion on State obligations concerning climate change.”
The ITLOS opinion derives from UNCLOS Article 138 and the ITLOS Statute Article 21, requested by an international organisation (COSIS) authorised by the UNGA. It interprets treaty obligations specific to the marine environment. The ICJ opinion stems from UN Charter Article 96 and the ICJ Statute Article 65, requested by the UNGA itself, addressing general international law obligations (including human rights, UNFCCC, customary law). Both are advisory and non‑binding, but the ITLOS opinion creates a focused precedent for law‑of‑the‑sea disputes, while the ICJ opinion has broader systemic reach. Enforceability in both cases relies on State compliance and subsequent judicial reference; neither creates direct enforcement mechanisms.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for “legal significance” of an advisory opinion, structure the answer in three layers: (1) source of jurisdiction and requestor, (2) substantive findings and their novelty, (3) normative impact on treaty regimes, State practice, and future litigation. Use a two‑column table to contrast ITLOS vs ICJ if both appear in the same question.

The UN Global Compact for Migration and the Global Compact on Refugees: Governance Architecture and Review Processes

Adopted in December 2018, the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM) and the Global Compact on Refugees (GCR) represent the first comprehensive, non‑binding frameworks negotiated under UN auspices to address large‑scale human mobility. The GCM, negotiated under the auspices of the UN General Assembly, comprises 23 objectives covering the entire migration cycle, from root‑cause mitigation to return and reintegration. The GCR, developed under UNHCR leadership, operationalises the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework (CRRF) through four pillars: easing pressures on host countries, enhancing refugee self‑reliance, expanding access to third‑country solutions, and supporting conditions in countries of origin for safe return.

Both compacts establish distinct but complementary follow‑up mechanisms. The GCM’s review architecture centres on the International Migration Review Forum (IMRF), convened every four years at the UN Headquarters, preceded by regional reviews and a multi‑stakeholder hearing. The first IMRF took place in May 2022, producing a Progress Declaration that highlighted gaps in data disaggregation, migrant‑worker protection, and access to basic services. The GCR’s follow‑up relies on the Global Refugee Forum (GRF), held every four years (first in 2019, second in 2023), where States and stakeholders announce pledges and contributions. The GRF 2023 generated over 1,600 pledges, including financial commitments exceeding USD 2.5 billion, and launched the “Responsibility‑Sharing Index” to track burden‑sharing equity.

Governance differs: the GCM is overseen by the UN Network on Migration (established 2018), a coordination platform of 38 UN entities, while the GCR is steered by UNHCR with the “Three‑Year Strategy on Resettlement and Complementary Pathways”. Both compacts emphasise whole‑of‑society engagement, yet implementation remains uneven. Common challenges include the voluntary nature of pledges, limited parliamentary oversight, and the absence of a binding dispute‑settlement mechanism. For examiners, the key distinction lies in the legal character: the GCM is a General Assembly‑endorsed political declaration, whereas the GCR is a UNHCR‑facilitated framework anchored in the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol. Questions often test the ability to map each compact’s objectives to specific SDG targets (e.g., GCM Objective 6 SDG 8.8; GCR Pillar 2 SDG 1.3).

The World Bank Pandemic Fund: Governance Structure, Financing Modalities, and Early Operations

Launched at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in June 2022 and formally operationalised in September 2023, the Pandemic Fund (officially the Financial Intermediary Fund for Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response) is hosted by the World Bank with the World Health Organization as technical lead. Its governing board comprises 20 voting members: 10 sovereign contributors (including the G7, Indonesia, South Africa, and the European Commission), 5 recipient‑country representatives, 3 civil‑society organisations, and 2 private‑sector/philanthropic representatives. The Board is co‑chaired by a donor and a recipient representative, ensuring balanced decision‑making.

Financing follows a “pay‑in” model: donors make legally binding contributions, which are pooled and allocated through a competitive call‑for‑proposals process. As of March 2024, the Fund had secured USD 2.0 billion in pledges, with USD 1.2 billion paid in. The first call (January‑March 2024) prioritised three investment areas: (i) strengthening zoonotic disease surveillance and laboratory capacity; (ii) building resilient health‑workforce and supply‑chain systems; (iii) enhancing community‑level risk communication and equity‑focused preparedness. Eligibility extends to low‑ and lower‑middle‑income countries, with a dedicated “fragile and conflict‑affected” window. Grants are disbursed through implementing entities (WHO, FAO, UNICEF, regional development banks) that meet fiduciary standards.

The Fund’s design incorporates lessons from the COVID‑19 response: a results‑based financing framework with pre‑agreed indicators, a rapid‑approval track for emergencies (decision within 30 days), and a “no‑regret” clause allowing reallocation of uncommitted funds to emerging threats. However, early critiques highlight the modest capitalisation relative to the estimated USD 10‑15 billion annual financing gap identified by the G20 High‑Level Independent Panel, and the absence of a replenishment calendar. For exam purposes, candidates should be able to contrast the Pandemic Fund with the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (disease‑specific, performance‑based) and the World Bank’s IDA Crisis Response Window (country‑level, concessional). The Fund’s governance model — multi‑stakeholder board, WHO technical leadership, World Bank fiduciary hosting — is a frequent case study in “innovative global health financing” questions.

The G20 Women’s Empowerment and Gender Equality Working Group: Mandate, Deliverables, and Linkages to SDG 5

Established under the Indian G20 Presidency in 2023, the Women’s Empowerment and Gender Equality Working Group (WG) institutionalised gender mainstreaming within the G20’s Sherpa and Finance tracks. The WG’s mandate, endorsed by the 2023 New Delhi Leaders’ Declaration, covers four priority pillars: (1) women’s economic participation and financial inclusion; (2) gender‑responsive budgeting and fiscal policy; (3) prevention and response to gender‑based violence; (4) women’s leadership in climate action and digital transformation. The WG reports jointly to the Development Working Group (DWG) and the Finance Track’s Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion (GPFI).

Key deliverables from the 2023 cycle include: the “G20 Policy Framework on Women’s Financial Inclusion”, which sets voluntary targets for member economies to close the gender gap in account ownership by 2030; a “Gender‑Responsive Budgeting Toolkit” co‑developed with UN Women and the OECD, piloted in six G20 countries; and the “G20 Compact on Preventing Gender‑Based Violence”, committing signatories to allocate a minimum of 0.5 % of ODA to GBV prevention programmes. The WG also launched a “Women in STEM” data portal, aggregating sex‑disaggregated indicators on research funding, patenting, and leadership across G20 members.

Operationally, the WG functions through a troika of co‑chairs (current, previous, incoming presidencies) and a secretariat hosted by the OECD. Its workplan is synchronised with the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW) and the High‑Level Political Forum (HLPF) to avoid duplication. The 2024 Brazilian Presidency expanded the WG’s scope to include care‑economy valuation and intersectional approaches for indigenous and Afro‑descendant women. For aspirants, the critical analytical point is the WG’s “soft‑law” character: its outputs are non‑binding political commitments, yet they create peer‑pressure benchmarks that feed into IMF Article IV gender‑clause assessments and World Bank Country Partnership Frameworks. Typical exam questions ask to map WG pillars to specific SDG 5 targets (e.g., Pillar 1 5.a, 5.b; Pillar 3 5.2) and to evaluate the effectiveness of voluntary G20 gender commitments versus treaty‑based obligations under CEDAW.

  • Confusing the UPR’s “noted” recommendations with “rejected” ones — “noted” implies the State acknowledges the recommendation but does not commit to implementation, whereas “rejected” is an explicit refusal.
  • Assuming the ITLOS advisory opinion creates a new treaty obligation — it interprets existing UNCLOS provisions; it does not amend the Convention.
  • Treating the GCM and GCR as legally binding instruments — both are non‑binding political frameworks; their force derives from moral and political commitment, not treaty law.
  • Equating the Pandemic Fund’s governance with that of the Global Fund — the Pandemic Fund’s board includes recipient‑country and civil‑society voting members, while the Global Fund’s board is constituency‑based with equal donor/recipient representation.
  • Believing the G20 Women’s Empowerment Working Group’s targets are mandatory for all members — they are voluntary policy benchmarks; compliance is monitored through peer review, not enforcement.
  • Overlooking the distinction between the UPR’s mid‑term reporting pilot (voluntary) and the treaty bodies’ mandatory periodic reporting cycles.
  • The ITLOS opinion’s reference to the 1.5 °C pathway does not impose a specific emissions‑reduction target on each State; it establishes a due‑diligence standard informed by the best available science.

The UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review: Mechanism, Mid‑Term Reporting Pilot, and Emerging Compliance Trends

The Universal Periodic Review (UPR) was established by General Assembly resolution 60/251 in 2006 as a peer‑review mechanism that examines the human rights records of all 193 UN member states every 4.5 years. Each review cycle consists of three stages: (1) submission of a national report, a compilation of UN information, and a summary of stakeholder submissions; (2) an interactive dialogue in the UPR Working Group where states pose questions and make recommendations; (3) adoption of an outcome report at the subsequent Human Rights Council session, where the state under review indicates which recommendations it “accepts” (commits to implement) and which it “notes” (acknowledges without commitment).

Since the third cycle (2017‑2021) the Council introduced a voluntary mid‑term reporting pilot, allowing states to submit an interim update on implementation of accepted recommendations. As of the 2023 pilot review, 38 states had submitted mid‑term reports, and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) published a synthesis noting that mid‑term reporting correlates with higher implementation rates for recommendations on civil and political rights. The pilot remains optional; the 2024 Council resolution 55/12 encouraged but did not mandate participation.

Compliance trends show a persistent gap between acceptance and implementation. OHCHR’s 2023 “UPR Implementation Tracker” indicates that only 42 % of accepted recommendations across all cycles have been fully implemented, with the lowest rates in economic, social and cultural rights (28 %). The Council’s “Voluntary Fund for Participation in the UPR” has expanded to support least‑developed countries in preparing national reports, yet capacity constraints remain a structural bottleneck. For exam purposes, candidates should be able to distinguish the UPR’s political, non‑binding character from the legally binding reporting obligations under the core human rights treaties, and to explain how the mid‑term pilot attempts to bridge the accountability gap without creating new legal obligations.

The World Trade Organization's Trade and Environment Committee: Environmental Goods Agreement Negotiations, Fisheries Subsidies Follow‑Up, and the 2023 Ministerial Outcomes

The WTO Committee on Trade and Environment (CTE) serves as the standing forum for dialogue on the intersection of trade rules and environmental policies. Its mandate, derived from the 1994 Marrakesh Decision on Trade and Environment, includes reviewing the environmental implications of WTO agreements and identifying areas where trade liberalisation can support sustainable development. The Committee meets in regular and special sessions, and its work feeds into Ministerial Conferences.

The Environmental Goods Agreement (EGA) negotiations were launched in 2014 by a coalition of 18 participants representing 46 WTO members, aiming to eliminate tariffs on a list of 54 environmental goods such as solar panels, wind turbines, and wastewater treatment equipment. Negotiations stalled in 2016 over disagreements on product coverage and the definition of “environmental goods”. A revived plurilateral effort in 2021 produced a revised list of 101 products, but consensus on a final text has not been reached. The 2023 CTE special session highlighted that the lack of a most‑favoured‑nation (MFN) extension clause remains a key sticking point, as non‑participants would not automatically benefit from tariff cuts.

On fisheries subsidies, the CTE monitors implementation of the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies adopted at the 12th Ministerial Conference (MC12) in June 2022. The Agreement prohibits subsidies for illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing and for overfished stocks, with a transition period for developing members. The 2023 CTE report noted that 71 members had ratified the Agreement by December 2023, triggering its entry into force once two‑thirds of members (110) deposit instruments of acceptance. The Committee also oversees the “Special and Differential Treatment” (S&DT) provisions, including the 2023 decision to extend the transition period for least‑developed countries by two years.
